utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we'll hear the Prosecution's response to the Defence Rule 98 bis submission. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. President and Your Honours, I will respond to the 98 bis submissions in the following order: First, addressing the three components in the order of municipalities, Sarajevo, Srebrenica and then addressing the submissions with respect to Count 1 and with respect to Count 11. During the course of some of my references, we'll have occasion to make reference to either evidence elicited during closed session or evidence that is under seal. Rather than moving repeatedly in and out of private session and public session, it's my intention to attempt to paraphrase or synopsise that evidence in a manner that doesn't intrude on the confidentiality concerns, if that is permissible with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Chamber sees no problem, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no objection from the Defence either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I'd like to move forward now to address some of the specific assertions with respect to Counts 3 through 8, focussing on events in municipalities in particular including -- and in Srebrenica in some respects. But before addressing some of the specific assertions and, indeed, misrepresentations made during the course of the Defence submissions, I'd like to note that all of those are made against the backdrop of evidence that demonstrates overwhelmingly that the Prosecution submissions and the indictment have been more than amply satisfied. And that evidence includes the following. First, the accused sought an ethnically pure state or a state as ethnically pure as he could make it. And in that respect, you can turn to the evidence of Ambassador Okun [Realtime transcript read in error "Owe"] who explained that one of the Bosnian Serb war-time goals "as enunciated to us directly" was to have their own state that would be as ethnically pure Serb or as overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb as they could make it. That's P776 and also at transcript reference 4157 through 58. He noted that the Bosnian Serb side was quite open and honest with us about these goals. And thank's at T1475. Now, of course, as Ambassador Okun also point out there was "no way that you could separate the peoples expect by force." You'll find that at T4354 through 55 and that's exactly what the Bosnian Serb forces set about doing. You can also find similar references in the testimony of David Harland who explained that the accused openly said that the basic war aim was to redistribute the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina so that the Serbs would be left in control of a single contiguous block of territory embracing the whole of the border with Serbia and Montenegro and also many areas that they deemed traditionally Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, can I interrupt for one moment. For the record, lines 15 and 21 of previous pages, "Ambassador Owe" should read O-k-u-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is correct. That reference to Mr. Harland is found at P820, paragraph 269. He also noted that the purpose of the continual pressure applied by the accused to extract concessions from the Bosnian Serb government was to force an acceptance of the redistribution of the populations; that is, the "ethnic cleansing" that had been achieved by the Bosnian Serb forces. See paragraph 270. And you'll also find from the evidence of Witness KDZ240 that the accused openly explained that the objective was the control by the Bosnian Serbs of a vast amount, 70 per cent, of Bosnia's territory with a homogenous population of Serbs. You can find that also at P2935 at page 6752. Now, those were goals that were communicated, promulgated to the accused's followers. As one example among many in the vast amount of evidence you have, you can turn to a statement by one of the delegates of the Assembly at the 34th Session of the Bosnian Serbs Assembly at page 33 through 34 who was responding to complaints by fellow delegates about the amount of territory that the Serbs might -- Bosnian Serbs might be allocated. And he suggested that they compare their gains and losses with the gains and losses of the Muslims and Croats and concluded: "Gentlemen there is no Serbian state in the Bosnian pot without gradual depopulation and relocating. If we want ethnically pure Serbian state, and we do, don't we, if we all know and emphasise that we cannot live with them then we have to realise that these draft maps are offering exactly that and there has to be relocation." Now, I alluded to the fact that this ethnically pure state, this homogenisation, this redistribution of populations was to take place over a vast amount of territory. And perhaps we can take a quick look at a few visual images that capture the extent of the territory that the accused considered to be Bosnian Serb and that had to be subjected to this need for homogenisation. First, we see a video image of the accused close confidant and compatriot, Mr. Krajisnik, standing before an ethnic map that captures the -- or reflects the territory taken, held and conquered by the Bosnian Serbs by late 1992. And as you can see from the horseshoe image, it indeed covers the amount of territory that the accused said and if you look to the previous references I made with respect to -- to -- to KDZ240 will you find that that is what the accused was saying in April, the beginning of the -- the commencement of the conflict was to be Bosnian Serb territory. And keep that image in mind when we turn to the other images which are reflections of - and that's P2561 - the map depicting the strategic objectives. So you can see objective 2 that covers the northern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina; 3, that covers the eastern part; 4, you'll see down in the south-eastern part and also in the west, the Una, and, of course, you're familiar with Sarajevo. And then if we can turn to the ethnic map, one of the ethnic maps of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's P797, I believe. You can see, for example, on the eastern part how that map depicts who lives in those areas. The green reflects a Muslim majority area, Muslim majority of such places as you see on the map as Bratunac, Srebrenica, Zvornik, Vlasenica, et cetera. And it's instructive to turn to a statement by the accused at the 53rd Bosnian Serb Assembly Session at pages 68 through 69 - and just for the record this map is P783 - he said -- and that was an assembly session in 1995. And this is what the accused had to say about that area: "To tell the truth, there are towns we grabbed for ourselves and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns we made up of 70 per cent. Don't there let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance they had to become ours and no one is practically questioning it anymore." So very quickly that depicts the areas that were sought by the accused and the objectives for those areas. And who was the accused as we've learned very clearly? He was the supreme commander, not just the supreme political leader but also the supreme military leader of Republika Srpska; first, of the Bosnian Serb movement in the form of the SDS and then in its formal structures. And for that, you have a wealth of evidence. You can turn to such evidence as the testimony of General Milovanovic at transcript pages 25444 through 445, who said: "The one and only superior of General Ratko Mladic was Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the republic. Dr. Radovan Karadzic was the supreme commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska." And then he explained what that meant. That meant that he commanded the army through Ministry of Interior. He commanded the police and indeed he commanded through the man who was in charge of civil protection, the civilian protection. You heard from General Srkbic, another member of the Main Staff, at transcript pages 26023, through 24, that the accused was the supreme commander in both peacetime and war time. General Gvero at the 19th Session of the Bosnian-Serb Assembly at pages 63 through 64 outlined the basic elements of the chain of command, and basically the elements are the president of the republic. At the time it was the Presidency as the supreme commander. All the elements of the defence and the army are subordinated to this institution. At the 34th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly at pages 315, General Mladic made clear that there wasn't a single order of the accused he hadn't obeyed. At the same session, one of the delegates, Mr. Milanovic, noted that the accused had taken on supreme executive and all other power upon himself and questioned whether that was a sensible thing to do since maybe he couldn't do everything. The accused himself made it clear. At the 39th Session pages 85 through 86, he said: "I am in charge, in particular of the army. Commanders report to me, commander of the Main Staff and commanders of corps and brigades. I am the one who signs, who decides and I will be responsible for each decision." You can also look at P3041 where there's a document from General Milovanovic indicating that orders can only come from the Main Staff and from the supreme commander of the RS armed forces, that is, Dr. Karadzic and from nobody else. And we know what those forces did. As just the tip of the iceberg, I turn the Court's attention of testimonies of three individuals and I have you look at, for example, P0457, page 43, which reflects the "ciscenje" of the Brdo area in Prijedor during which thousands of Muslims were rounded up by the VRS and police. And "ciscenje" which is traditionally translated here as either mopping up or cleansing, or, on some occasions, the translators carefully note mopping up or cleansing. The witness explained that in this instances, "ciscenje" meant specifically that the Muslim population had to be removed. Or turn to P3634 at page 72 which discusses the "cleansing of various villages in Sanski Most and the expulsion of "all the Muslims" by the VRS. Or turn to P3227 which describes the cleansing by the joint forces of the VRS and the police of various villages in Vlasenica, including the roundup of all Muslims, the routine killing of males and the burning of houses. And you can look at page 12 for that. And makes reference to the explanation by a commander, "Well" -- about why the burning: "Well, can you see for yourselves that if we don't set fire to those houses they'll return later on." Find that at page 13. Now, Your Honours, those references were to cleansings by the accused's forces in very late May or June or July. Now I'll turn to cleansing operations some months later and I'll specifically discuss the accused's involvement in those particular events, and as an interesting chronology that the Court has had an opportunity to observe. So first we see that on the 8th of November, 1992, the accused, Mr. Krajisnik and others met with General Mladic and corps commanders, including Drina Corps Commander Zivanovic. And if you turn -- you'll see at P1481, a portion of the Mladic diary - that's at e-court page 146 through 147 - Mr. Krajisnik explains that not all of the strategic objectives have been achieved. They have achieved the corridor; that's through Operation Corridor up in -- in part in north-west Bosnia. But Mr. Krajisnik explains, The most pressing thing is to mop up Orasje, a heavily Croat area up north, and then to solve the problem of the Podrinje area and the Neretva valley as soon as possible. The Muslims must not stay with us and they should not be given any kind of autonomy. The important objective is the task assigned to Zivanovic the mopping up of the Drina, the "ciscenje" of the Drina. The most important task is separation from the Muslims. Now we also learned that in the days following, the accused was asked to review and approve directive 4 and offered suggestions and verbally approved it and returned it for signature. That's D02149. Directive 4 was indeed issued on November 19th, and as they had discussed on the 8th, it orders operations to reach the left bank of the Neretva, page 4, to "liberate Orasje, meaning that they didn't have it yet but wanted it. That's page 5. And with respect to what Mr. Krajisnik had explained on the 8th as the most important task, the one to be given to Zivanovic, the "ciscenje" of the Drina, this order: "The rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region are to exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on them and force them to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas with the Muslim population." P976, page 5. Now, and on the following day, Mladic ordered that a seminar regarding the activities and tasks for the Drina Corps be prepared in response to a specific request by the accused and it was to be led personally by the accused. And you can find that at P3037, P4921. This conference was held on the 23rd of November. That's P4922. And the syllabus and the schedule reveal that the accused opened the seminar and -- or conference and after hearing from various commanders, including Zivanovic, gave the closing speech and gave the tasks for the work of the Drina Corps and the organs of the civilian government. That's P4248. You will also find in the accused's own diary in handwritten notes the tasks given to Zivanovic. And it says "Colonel Zivanovic: Tasks:" And a number of items, Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. That's P2716. And the following day, the 24th of November, Zivanovic issued the following order: "Pursuant to directive of the Main Staff," et cetera, et cetera, "I have decided, 1, launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." The "ciscenje" of the Drina, to render it clean, just as the strategic objective number 3 and as Krajisnik had explained, envisaged. Now before leaving that, I want to turn quickly to a few reflections of the nature of the operations that resulted, and the Court has P5261, an intercept dated the 8th of February, 1993, between Zivanovic and Gborevic [phoen]. And Zivanovic says, Hold tightly the positions. Are the Turks' houses burning? And Gborevic says, They're burning. They're burning. And Zivanovic says, Way to go, as many as possible. Or P3162, that's a Birac Light Infantry -- Infantry Brigade combat report signed by Svetozar Andric who would later become the chief of staff of the Drina Corps, promoted by the accused in the middle of the Srebrenica genocide. Our forces which are moving in the wider area of Kamenica, Gajici, and Grobici [phoen] worked according to plan without major problems. The village of Gobulje [phoen] has been burnt and tomorrow the plan is to do Poljevine [phoen]. Or P3161, another Andric document: "In the course of the day special units of the 1st Birac Brigade took and destroyed the village of Gobili [phoen], thus freeing up the left bank of the main forces in the attack on Cerska. At the entry into the village, our soldiers found weapons and other military equipment as well as food and cattle which the enemy left behind when fleeing from our forces." And the accused and his confidant, Mr. Krajisnik, kept their eye on the ball with respect to strategic objective number 3 and there perceived need to clean the Drina. As Krajisnik said at the 33rd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly: "Since Vojo Kupresanin has asked me this question, I believe we have to understanding something. We have strategic goals. Just imagine how the people of Herzegovina would be angry because the Neretva is not our river. Just imagine how angry they would be -- or how they would be angry because we haven't cleaned the Drina, and imagine how others would be angry because we don't have a part of the Sarajevo." The accused would later remind people of exactly the same thing. At the 53rd Session at page 68, he said: "The Drina should be clean." Now that's merely part of the backdrop against which the assertions made by the accused in their submission of Monday must be understood, but, nevertheless, I'd like to address some of the specific assertions that were made. At -- on Monday, at transcript page 28581, the accused somehow tried to analogise or to assert that the population movement was simply a matter of -- that could be analogised to a hurricane, like a -- Katarina or some -- like in other countries, if there's a natural disaster, if there's a hurricane in the US coast, there has to be an evacuation. And tried to suggest that was the nature of the population redistribution that took place in territories claimed by his political and military forces. Of course, that gives rise to any number of follow-up questions, such as why was there active destruction of virtually all of the religious sites and mosques in those territories. You heard the testimony of Mr. Riedlmayer and you saw in Exhibit P4070 which documents the destruction of 281 mosques in 22 municipalities located in the territory seized and held by the accused's forces during the period of the indictment. You heard also among many other pieces of information, specific information from specific municipalities relating to mosques, the testimony of Milan Tupajic and Exhibit P05238 about the destruction of mosques in the Sokolac municipality by the engineers of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. He also explained why: "There's a belief among the Serbs that if there are no mosques, there are no Muslims and by destroying the mosques, the Muslims will lose a motive to return to their villages." As another example, again, among many, you can turn to P3634 which is under seal which reflects information to essentially the same effect that information was put out to the effect that if you destroy a Muslim religious site and set fire to his house he'll never go back. That information was put out by Crisis Staff members. And the destruction of mosques was to eradicate or delete all traces of Muslim presence in the area and, of course, to intimidate the remaining Muslims into leaving the area. The ethnic cleansing was the reason for the destruction of the mosques. And after natural disasters it doesn't typically happen that the names of the towns and municipalities are changed to reflect their Serbian domination. For example, you heard -- you can see at P3478 that after Kozarac, a town that was 700 years old, was burned down, the soldiers put up a sign calling it Radmilova, that is, in the Cyrillic alphabet, named after the Bosnian Serb military figure who had cleansed and burned what -- what was up to then, a Muslim town. Or the testimony of KDZ379 at transcript page 18851 through 52, that after the war, towns were given names with Serbian prefixes and they assigned their own names to places based on their decisions. Or P3476 where you can see Miroslav Stanic from Foca -- Foca local leader, describing his role as both a member of the Main Board of the SDS and the president of the Municipal Board of what had up to then had been Foca and what had become Srbinje. And, indeed, you can hear the accused's view on that as well, if you turn to the 37th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly at page 110 where he said: "Two years ago, we were a group in Bosnia and Herzegovina that had some rights, and now we are the state. And what we hold is 100 per cent ours. Look at Srbinje. Their plans for Srbinje were to build a big Islamic centre there. Foca is extremely important to them but it will never be theirs again." And after a natural disaster, you're unlikely to see an effort by the authorities in power to affirmatively cement the population redistribution that resulted and prevent the return of the people who previously lived there. There are many examples of that, but an extremely interesting one that this Court had an opportunity to see at two separate Assembly Sessions involving the accused specifically and his plans to effect that occur in two Assembly Sessions. First, the 37th Assembly Session in January of 1994 where there's a colloquy between the accused and Mr. Maksimovic, a significant Bosnian Serb political official who was the president of the Deputies Club in 1991 and 1992, and Maksimovic says at pages 126 through 127 is that he wants to see a firm attitude that the Muslims and Croats will not be allowed to return: "I do not care if the Muslims will live at all, where they will live, whether they will have a country or not. The only thing I'm interested in is my people and the territory where my people live. Therefore any thought about having 500 or more Muslims within our future country is out of the question." And the accused responds that with respect to the return of refugees that he owes an answer to Vojo's question. He notes that according to international law, they can't specifically ban the return of return the refugees, and they can -- in principle, they can return. But he would add just one sentence. This also has to be a two-way process. And he knows that later on one of the internationals asked him, Why did you insist on a two-way process? And he says, When then the Serbs from Zvornik returned to Zenica, then the Muslims from Prijedor will return to Prijedor. Therefore, it must be a two-way process. And at the 53rd, he explained it even more carefully and explicitly. Again, he was -- that's at -- that's at the 53rd Assembly Session, and that's Exhibit P988. That's at page 29. Again, he is talking about the insistence by the international community on a right of return. And he notes that we have added must be an overall process. And the internationals don't quite know what that's about. So he's -- explains, What does that mean an overall process? That means that the Muslims from Kozluk can return to Kozluk if the Serbs from Kozluk return to Zenica. If they don't want to return then we -- if they cannot return then we need a new war to exchange that, and that's why we should always insist on this; so an overall process, either overall or not at all. We can act the Serbian Cyrillic way and tell it to their face or we can be a bit cunning. We do have to be a bit cunning. So that was how he intended to cement the cleansing. And you might ask yourselves, Well, how exactly he spoke about the Muslims from Kozluk? How did they leave in the first place? You have that information - if you turn to P1478 - that's the Mladic notebook. It reflects a meeting that General Mladic had with the accused and representatives from Zvornik and other municipalities on 30th of June, 1992. And take a look at that document because two representatives from Zvornik talk about that, one is a political representative, Mr. Grujic, one was the TO commander, Mr. Pavlovic. Grujic says, We have successfully implemented the president's decision to settle Divic and Kozluk with our children. And Pavlovic explains -- that's at pages 246 through 247. Pavlovic explains at page 250 through 251, indeed, boasts to his Commander-in-Chief, We were most active in evicting the Muslims. We have brought peace to Sepak, Divic and Kozluk. Some of them wanted to move out, while we demanded it. We had to evict some of the people also for the sake of our heros who fled from Kovacevici. And you also heard evidence from a victim from one of those who was forced to leave his home in order to implement the president's decision, and that was Mr. -- you can find that at P00104, Mr. Banjanovic, pages 23 through 24, and he explains the cleansing of Kozluk and how Muslims were forced to leave in the presence of thousands of soldiers who made it crystal-clear when you read that statement that the Muslims were obliged to leave the area. I had referred to the accused's explanation of how he was going to ensure that Muslim did not return. He also explained on the same occasion, as he had on previous occasions, why, and at page 33, you can see that he says that they have to draw a hard-line because they're worried about Muslims leaving the Muslim part and coming back to the Serb part: If they can live on Grbavica, if they can leave in Doboj, they can live anywhere and we have to prevent it. Now, the accused also said on Monday, or asserted on Monday, that the war and violence were not fundamental preconditions for implementing the objectives. On the contrary the objectives were recognised by the international community and they could be attained without going to war. He said that the Serbs were not prepared for war and they had no -- neglected to make any preparations, et cetera. Well, with regard to preparations and the assertions that no preparations were made, you can turn to an enormous wealth of material about the efforts undertaken by the accused to make sure that the Bosnian Serbs were amply prepared, and, indeed, at the -- I think the 11th Assembly Session, he asserts that, We have taken all measures necessary to ensure. We haven't neglected to take those measures, contradicting what he tries to tell the Court here. But look also at the 50th Assembly Session and see these comments from Jovan Tintor from Vogosca, and that's at page 304. And he speaks about the period of time before the war and explains his role: "I was ordered to create military formations. Perhaps you do not know it, General," and he's speaking to Mladic here, "but I want you to know this. I went from municipality to municipality and created military formations on order from my president. And this is true. Here are people who know this to be the truth and have papers to prove it. We created brigade commanders down to platoon commanders. All this was done by SDS for the good of the Serbian people and all this we did as best we could." Now, just to confirm that Mr. Tintor, while he may be boasting, he is telling the truth. That's confirmed by the accused himself - at pages 2323 to 2324 - who says, I will say that when it all began the Serbian people was ready, more ready than ever. There was a brigade or a detachment in each municipality. There was a command hidden from the JNA, although not so much here. Now, the accused stated on Monday, or suggested on Monday, as he had on other occasions, that the strategic objectives were -- had nothing to do with the military efforts and were simply a reflection of the negotiating positions taken by the Bosnian Serbs during 1992. It is impossible to enumerate all the documentation, all the statements, of which indicate the contrary, but let me touch upon a few. First of all is the obvious fact that the accused consulted with Mladic before enunciating the strategic objectives. If you turn to the Mladic diary you will see a meeting on May 6, the accused, Mr. Krajisnik, General Mladic working out the strategic objectives. You'll find that at P1477, pages 256 through 258. At the 16th Session of the Assembly on May 12, Mladic would explain that he worked on the strategic objectives. Listen -- well, and then Mladic at the 34th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in 1993 was equally explicit: "First, the people and the army with the help from the rest of us, according to our possibilities, have carried out most of the tasks and strategic goals sent to them. We have created Republika Srpska." And at the 50th Session he would confirm the same thing. You find that at page 22: "The tasks of the army in this war stem from the known six strategic objectives, adopted by our Assembly which have not been carried out to the full due to lack of material and other support." General Milovanovic who you heard from, if you look at D2149 - it was actually a Defence exhibit - explained that at some point during the war the accused relieved the VRS of the responsibility to solve the Neretva - that's strategic objective number 4 - in the military way, and Milovanovic's only regret that he didn't ask whether or not it was the case that the -- because they were having similar problems it was the case that the VRS was no longer tasked with carrying out the implementation of strategic objective number 6, that is access to the sea. You can also look directly at the words of the combat readiness report signed off on and with a long editorial portion by the accused himself which states -- and that's D325. You can find that at page 159: "The strategic objectives of the war were handed down to the VRS Main Staff, not specific tasks and operations, and the objectives served as general guide-lines of the actual operations. However, the president of the republic did issue some specific tasks orally, if they were of vital importance." And that goes on at page 160: In the last month and a half, the operations have concentrated on the liberation of Vodrije [phoen], and thereby, the strategic objective of our war be realised, one that could be defined as establishing contact with Serbia on the river Drina or the Drina ceasing to be a frontier." And that's a reflection of some of the operations stemming from directive 4 that I referred to at the beginning of our discussion. Among the other preparations made by the accused beyond those discussed by Tintor himself at the 50th, of course, were the -- the establishment of the executive bodies necessary to implement the strategic objectives in each municipality, a good deal of which was set up through the intervention of the Variant A and B document, the instructions for the organs, the activities of organs in an emergency condition. So that's -- sets up Crisis Staffs and tells them sequentially what they are to do and to get ready for what -- what might happen. The accused has tried hard not only on Monday to suggest there were no preparations. But also during the course of the case, I couldn't possibly hope to go over all the information related to Variant A and B document, but I do want to touch upon a little just to underscore that the accused's effort to mischaracterise his role in that document. So you -- and here's some -- only some of the evidence. You heard from witnesses that it was the accused who distributed the document. You can turn to P2568 at transcript 16647, 16650, that's Mr. Neskovic, about the accused's distribution of the document. You heard from Prstojevic about how the document was distributed at that -- at that time. You saw considerable evidence of how it was received and immediately implemented by various municipalities. Can you turn to P2575, P2595 P5517, P2592, P2590, P2589, and I'm referring to such municipalities as Prijedor, Kljuc, Novo Sarajevo, Bratunac and Zvornik. And you also saw evidence of the accused's immediate role in ensuring the implementation of that document. That's seen through, among other things, a series of intercepts where the accused, first he talks to someone asking for Cizmovic, that's D1434, on the 20th. Then he speaks with Krajisnik about the need to have Cizmovic run from municipality to municipality. P2550 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, take a look at the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are kindly asked to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I actually speak to the -- my apologies to the reporter and I spoke to the interprets before in the hope that I would avoid that. I'll just mention a few more slowly. There are intercepts reflecting the accused's discussions with Cizmovic including explicit references to the need to travel from municipality to municipality to ensure that the instructions are implemented. And you can look at P2551, 2552, 2553, 2552, Cizmovic says -- he talks about -- he is checking out how far had they come, to what extent are they prepared to implement the first level of the instructions. At the 6th Assembly Session on January 26 when they're discussing the need for urgent action, Cizmovic stands up in front of everybody, including the accused, and says -- calls for the urgent operationalisation and declaration of activities and that the tasks set out in the 19 December 1991 instruction should be carried out. It was explicitly activated. The second level of the instructions were explicitly activated by the accused on 14th of February. He refers to them four separate times, and says at page 24 of P00012: "That is why we called you today to intensify, to introduce the second level and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." And that is reflected also in P2597 and in P5516. Those were municipality reflections of that activation by the accused. And, finally, the accused himself at the 46th and 50th Sessions of the Assembly made specific references to the importance of Variant A and B in preparing the Bosnian Serbs for what would happen, and for what they needed to do. That's at 347 through 348 of the 46th Session. Do you remember the instruction A and instruction B, he asks them. We had Crisis Staffs, and it was clear that they were the authority. The people were not left without the authority because there was a Crisis Staff. And at the 50th Session, P970, at page 316, he says, You will remember the A and B Variants so that at the moment the war began in the municipalities where we were in the majority, where we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything, in the municipalities where we were in the minority we set up secret government, Municipal Boards, municipal assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. We had set up -- you will remember the A and B Variants. And the B Variant where we were in the minority, 20, 15 per cent, we had set up a government and a brigade, a unit no matter what size but there was a detachment with a commander. And he goes on at that same Session to describe how they created and liberated the space. Now, the accused also asserted that separation was not a declared aim and he was sort of focussing on the period of February and March. I think, in that instances, asking the Court to look at certain isolated statements made during that period before the conflict broke out when the two-track process of engaging in negotiations in the hope of obtaining resolution satisfactory to the Bosnian Serbs while simultaneously preparing for war if they didn't get what they wanted was taking place. And he tried to suggest that those statements should somehow trump the vast amount of evidence indicating the contrary. Just two documents -- a couple of documents clearly indicate what was happening there. First of all, at the 11th Assembly Session, the accused made explicit that -- why they had to say one thing to internationals and keep some other things secret, and he said: "We do not have to say everything yet," tis is at page 44, "the fact is that all the telescopes are now pointed at Yugoslavia, at Bosnia-Herzegovina. The ultimate strategic goal must still remain a secret." But when pressed, he made clear that separation, contrary to what he asserted on Monday, was indeed the objective. And for that, you have only have to look at P938. That is square in the middle of that February/March period. It is February 28th, 1992. And he said the following, and the context was he is insisting that a unified policy be followed so that there's no risk that in the Bosnian Serb territories some temporary solution will be reached that results in too many Muslims. And he says: "Imagine the stupidity of it. The conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina is basically a conflict among peoples. Just as it was in the case between Indian and Pakistan, and that's nothing new, it resulted in a huge resettlement of the people. Muslims cannot live with others, we must be clear on that. They couldn't life with the Hindu who are as peaceful as sheep." He goes on to describe the -- to continue to assert Muslims can't live with others. There can be no discuss here, he says. And he says -- and then he pushes against the possibility of a separate Bosnian Krajina, saying in two years' time, you would have problems against to separate each and every village there, "because they will overwhelm you with their birth-rate and their tricks, we cannot allow that to happen." And even after the ethnic cleansing had been largely achieved, you'll find at the 17th -- by the time that 17th Session of the Bosnian Serbs Assembly in July of 1992, the accused is boasting about having conquered approximately 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, indeed, acknowledging that there was territory they could consider give willing back in negotiations, and you saw the Krajisnik map which indicated the vast extent of the territories that were successfully conquered by the Bosnian Serb forces. And, by the way, when I use the term "conquering," it is not a term invented by the Prosecution. You will find it in various documents. For example, at the 16th Assembly Session, one of the delegates from Brcko in that case asks the accused to assist in getting more people to Brcko to assist in the conquering because in Brcko the Serbs were a minority. But even after all that had been accomplished, there was a continued emphasise on the need for national homogenisation. If you look at P794, you'll see a meeting in January of 1993 at the council for co-ordinating positions on state policy. The accused was there. Mr. Krajisnik was there. Mr. Koljevic was there and high-ranking officials, including Mr. Milosevic from Serbia. And there was this colloquy between the accused and the foreign minister of Serbia, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Jovanovic talks about the goals and says, The territorial link with -- and this is at page -- I'll have to get the pages that -- I think it is page 34, but I will have to check the precise page, Mr. President. Mr. Jovanovic says, The territorial link with Serbia Montenegro is hugely important, so it's not transitory, but: "What is more important is to make the territory that we get nationally homogenous as soon as possible. And that is the strategic goal to which they should aspire." He urges the Bosnian Serbs to refrain from ethnic cleansing to do that, that is, traditional ethnic cleansing, but explains how there are various ways of making it clear to people that they should leave the provinces that are controlled by the Serbs and go -- go elsewhere and Dr. Karadzic responds quite affirmatively and enthusiastically, I think that this which Jovanovic is talking about, that's already happened to a huge extent. He assures him, There was 50-50 of us in Zvornik and now the number of inhabitants of Zvornik is the same, approximately 50.000, and they're all Serbs. And that's all of a piece with his discussion with Mr. Maksimovic later about how he will ensure that it the Muslims cannot return. Similarly, in focussing on snippets from particular moments and documents taken from a particular context in order to emphasise something that is belied by the overall weight of the evidence, the accused focussed on -- he said on 22nd of April, I issued a platform suggesting that territories taken by force be not recognised and that peace be secured as soon as possible, and that the Prosecution hadn't shown that he supported the expansion of territory. Well, apart from the evidence that I've already recited, let me focus on that specific period, that is, the April time, where the accused wants you to focus for a moment and see what's happening. And for that, you can turn quickly to the two sources. The first is P1477, the Mladic notebook entry of the 6th of May, 1992. That's a meeting that I referred to earlier. At that meeting the accused explained to General Mladic, We are -- with respect to Sarajevo, We are controlling the Serbian settlements in the city and expanding them. It would be a disaster, he noted, if we did not separate with them. Controlling the Serbian settlements and expanding them. And that was confirmed, as you may recall, at the 17th Assembly Session, that's P28, which was held in July when one of the local Serbian Crisis Staff leaders -- Mr. Prstojevic had this to say about what was happening in Sarajevo, that at the very beginning, they didn't know whether Mr. Karadzic was alive: "During the first couple of days when we learned that he was alive and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been majority." So, contrary to the accused's suggestion, he was immediately and directly as he acknowledged to Mladic himself encouraging the expansion of Serbian -- Bosnian Serb territory. Mr. President, there's a great deal of additional material I want to cover. I hope to get back to it, but I want to stick to the timetable and be fair to the rest of the components of the case, so it may be a bit truncated. I'm about to move to the Sarajevo section. Two of the issues I had wished to cover, among others with respect to the accused's specific comments on Monday, was the suggestion that he didn't have contact with the municipalities or the opportunity for contact based on his references to the testimony of Mr. Djeric. In that respect, although I may be able to return it, I would simply say that if you look at the testimony and the -- of Mr. Djeric, he was talking about the fact that it was the government, way up there at the top of Mount Jahorina, distant from where the accused was that was out of contact, and he specifically noted in his statement the efforts he was making to get the people who did have communications and did have information to provide him with such, including the accused's right-hand men, Momcilo Mandic and Mr. Stanisic. And you heard ample evidence about the Bosnian Serb communication system including the VRS communication system, the republic communication system, which were merged and linked, and which was never -- the only time it was down was in August of 1995 briefly because of the NATO bombing and it functioned in various ways and the RS MUP system. For that you could look at P2794 for an extensive discussion about how those systems worked, and the other -- one of the other issues I would have hoped to cover and may be able to return to is the accused's effort to distance himself from the detention facilities, and suggesting that he both couldn't have known what was going on, didn't have information. Let me simply note that if you turn to, again, the testimony of Mr. Djeric, you will see considerable reference to that issue that by May -- by -- at the earliest stages beginning with a decision by the national security council of which the accused was head. A system of detention of civilians was set up. On the 8th of May, the republic exchange commission was established. That was a parametal structure that reached down through the regions to the municipalities. You can see that the -- you may remember the video of the Bratunac prisoners you saw - that was P3206; that was May 14th - who came through Pale -- were in Pale for a couple of days. They were, quote/unquote, "exchanged through the exchange commission," and if you look at the sessions of the Bosnian Serb government on June 10th and June 15th, you will see the extreme concerns about the risk of international condemnation about what was happening in such facilities that threatened the entire state if not handled correctly. And Djeric told you he -- they had information about that. Among other things, it prompted him to write a letter to James Baker, the US Secretary of State, on May 24th denying that, such camps existed. And that all of those were -- efforts were based on the information they were receiving about the mistreatment and -- and -- and inhumane conditions in -- in camps. And that would include intercepts between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Mandic and Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mandic about -- about prisons in camps. You can look at -- I'll get you those cites after the break, in fact. I think it's P1102 and P1103. There was a July 17th report by Mr. Stanisic, the president of the MUP, directly to Mr. Karadzic, talking about the fact that the army and the Crisis Staffs were rounding up Muslim civilians and placing them in inhumane conditions. Stanisic's concern, as you will see from that document, is not the crime that is taking place systematically but instead its impact on his own resources and the resources of the MUP. And the fact that nothing happened at all until the international community, as you heard from Mr. Vulliamy, exposed in a graphic way what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the condition of the camps, and even then people continued to languish in Manjaca and Batkovic and other facilities. Mr. President, I hope that it will be such that I'll be able to return to some of the specific assertions with respect to municipalities and Counts 3 through 8. But in the meantime, I want to turn to the accused's assertions about Counts 9 through 10, and about Sarajevo. Again, I intend to address some of the accused's specific assertions but all of that must be seen against the back drop of the overwhelming evidence about what took place in Sarajevo and who was responsible. We saw witness after witness with extensive military experience and/or experience in other conflicts who had the opportunity to observe and experience the shelling and sniping in Sarajevo over many months and who concluded that the campaign was intended to inflict terror on the population. KDZ185 concluded that the "prime objective" of the shelling and sniping was to terrorise the civilian population. And when asked why he chose the term "terror," he explained it. Explaining at transcript pages 4177 through 78 what the experience of being subjected to this as defenceless civilian without weapons must be like and how it must be contrasted to the experience of someone who at least would be able to do something about it. A contemporaneous report for July 8th, 1995, and it's a rather typical report states: "Sniping and mortaring are still at a reasonably high level. This seems to have no particular military value but contributes to a general atmosphere in the city. Almost no civilians now use the city's main east/west thoroughfare, that's sniper alley, so much so that snipers who used to work that area now seem to have relocated. Sporadic, almost random bombardment of the city continues." And the author of the report testify -- by the way, that's P822 at page 2. The author of the report testified here, that is Mr. Harland, and he said he wasn't trying to be emotional in using that term. He was merely trying to reflect what was happening and the feeling of the population as a result of the various levers of pressure applied, the shelling and sniping and the lack of humanitarian assistance, and so on. And terror was the word that witness after witness with military and combat experience used to describe the shelling and sniping in Sarajevo. van Baal, P1818; Adbul Razik, see transcript 5514 through 15; van Lynden, P926, paragraph 25; Bowen, transcript 10212 through 10213; Tucker, P4203, paragraph 90; Fraser, P1762, paragraph 73; Brennskag, P1851, paragraph 60; Banbury, P2451, paragraph 199; KDZ304, P2407, page 10; KDZ182, transcript 13038; and so on. And the evidence shows that the accused was clearly in overall command of this campaign, ratchetting the terror up and down as it suited his political aims. Banbury, for example, concluded that Mladic and Karadzic absolutely, that was his word, had the ability to modulate the level of terror in Sarajevo: "They could improve conditions by, for example, opening the airport, allowing commercial supplies, supplying gas, et cetera, stopping the sniping, stopping the shelling, and, equally, make conditions worse by restricting these things. Both men demonstrated such abilities by using them as leverage in negotiations." That's P2451, paragraph 200. And General Rose reached a similar conclusion. The parties at the senior military level on both sides have the ability to control the shelling and sniping as was evident through negotiating terms of the cessation of sniping, for example. He added that: "It was clear that Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic were at the peak of the pyramid of control of the Bosnian Serb forces." That's P1638. Paragraphs 205 through 207. These observations by the internationals are matched by the direct evidence of the accused's control of military actions in Sarajevo. So, for example, we see and we -- we had an opportunity to see the intercepted conversation of the 13th of August, 1993, where the accused directed General Gvero to order Galic to: "Pull the troops back far enough to avoid us having any problems in relation to the international community." And, further, that the information that has been done must reach Owen by 2.00 or 2.30, and moments later, Gvero assures Karadzic: "Both written and oral orders were issued to Galic and the chief has gone up there to personally check whether it has been done." That's P4783. General Galic implemented the order the same day. P5042. Indeed, the very nature of the campaign belies the accused's assertion that he was not in overall control of the shelling and sniping and the terror. Mr. Banbury observed: "In light of the longevity of the campaign of sniping and shelling and the ongoing notice provided there is no other conclusion to draw but that the campaign was the policy of Bosnian Serb leaders. The execution of the siege required vast resources and was on such a scale, such a large-scale, that it can only have be ordered from the highest levels." That's P2451, paragraph 203. And that observation also demonstrates that by continuing the campaign for well over three years, fully aware of impact, the accused intended to spread terror among the civilian population of Sarajevo. Now, on Monday, the accused asserted that the Prosecution "did not manage to prove that the Serbian side fired indiscriminately," did not manage to prove that the Serbs carried out militarily unjustified actions in the Sarajevo sector, and didn't manage to prove that Sarajevo was a civilian zone or that civilians were the target of any given military action by the Serb side. To the contrary, Your Honours, the evidence reveals that the shelling in Sarajevo was directed - was indeed largely directed - at the civilian population rather than military objects, and this is clear from a wealth of evidence. General Fraser explained that in the middle of the city there were no military positions. And when shelling happened inside the city: "We would go and investigate or the UNMOs would go in and investigate. And for the most part there were only civilian communities or people in those areas, no military target that we could identify." That is P1762, page 51. UNMO Thomas observed shelling into residential areas and: "Could see no military value in anything that was being shelled. There was no military target that they could be attacking with shells. It just seemed to be random into buildings." And Thomas added that the lack of military value to this shelling was underscored by the lack of any apparent target analysis by the Bosnian Serbs of what they had hid. Konings also -- and that is transcript pages 6798 through 6799. Konings also "observed that they just fired into civilian areas. They didn't care where the exact impact was. They were clearing harassing people over and over again." P1952, para 22. And then when asked whether he was aware of shelling of purely residential areas, KDZ182: "Of course. It is obvious there were areas which to my knowledge and to the knowledge of UNPROFOR as a whole, there was no military target. Those shellings aimed at the population." That's P13038 through 13039. Now, a number of witnesses with military backgrounds make a point of distinguishing between real military shelling which the Bosnian Serbs carried out in certain specific circumstances from the bulk of the shelling, which was "random" with no military purpose. For example, van Lynden distinguished "concentrated fire which accurately pounded the Marshal Tito Barracks" which was the type of carefully directed shelling one would expect to see in an army's attempt to destroy a particular target. He went on to say: "On the other hand, there was wild, scattered shelling going on all over the city. At the time it seemed to me that the second type of fire which did not appear to be concentrated on any particular target could only have been an expression of anger over losing the barracks or was meant to punish and frighten the population." KDZ185 also saw two types of shelling. The first, the more traditional type to support a military action; and the second, to increase psychological pressure on the population and also on the Bosnian government. So: "Then they were just firing at random on the city in a totally random fashion." Mr. Tucker's observations were similar. He said: "There were two types of incoming fire: There was concentrated fire, in other words multiple shells landing in a short space of time in a particular area; and the second type of fire was single shells landing arbitrarily around the city to no military purpose. These were shells which were just landing somewhere within Sarajevo, in other words, the built-up areas, civilian areas. They were not fired in support of attacks or to defend. They were simply fired into the city." And he explained that this random shelling was a "daily" occurrence. That's P4203, paragraph 23. Mr. Mole, Richard Mole, also testified that these "random" scattered rounds served no military purpose. And he would call it indiscriminate fire. He said this is a type of fire he observed in -- and that's at T5818 through 5819. He explained that this is the type of fire he observed in Sarajevo: "When I refer to shelling of the city, I refer to odd rounds landing all over the place. This is in contrast to concentrated fire. If there is a target and there is a fire mission to attack that target there will be a concentration of fire around that area." And he and his observers routinely reported random shelling of the city. That's P1435, on a variety of reports, 1433, 1434, 1429. As Brennskag explained to Your Honours: "In my experience, single rounds do not form part of a normal military offensive. They provide little or no military advantage. This indicates to me that the aim of such fire was not to hit military targets but instead to terrorise the civilian population." And he added that in June of 1995 the launching of such single rounds occurred several times a day resulting in purely civilian casualties. P1851, para 31. Konings provided similar explanation, noting many rounds are needed to destroy buildings. And when he and his team witnessed -- however were falling rounds in a random pattern not in a way that you combat military targets with: "The fact is what I saw is that they were random firing with single rounds or a few rounds on areas where there were no military targets whatsoever." That's T9345 through 9346. And General Wilson is another international who made similar observations. He said: "Typically the Serb fire would be spread over. It might be over a kilometre." He said, "mixture that the mixture of calibres, heavy and light, did no appear to be related to any particular tire -- target, no concentration of fire, you know, they didn't appear to have a specific target in mind. It was just the general area that was being fired upon." T4131. Now, another related phenomenon that the international military personnel and others saw was the massively disproportionate responses to Bosnian offensives and the punitive shelling of civilians in response to those offensives. General Wilson described them as: "Undoubtedly disproportion because of the volume and weight of fire and its wide distribution." And he would describe thousands of rounds being directed on an urban area in response to limited outgoing fire. That's P1029, paragraph 52. Tucker observed the same thing in response to Bosnia -- to Bosnian government attempts to break out of the siege and that the Bosnian Serb army would respond with heavy weapons to stabilise and then push back the Bosniaks. And then he said they would then carry out what we interpreted as punitive shelling of the city -- of the city out of which the infantry attack had been mounted and that sequence of events was observed time and time again. So what UNPROFOR observed and sensed was that this was an effort to "punish the citizens in the area from which the attack had come and to demonstrate how useless it was to resist." That's pipe 2403, para 91. Indeed, Richard Mole explained that on at least five to ten occasions, General Galic himself explicitly threatened to shell Sarajevo as retaliatory measure if events elsewhere did not go in the Serb's favour. And he described this behaviour as part of an "accepted norm." That if the Serb side failed to achieve their objectives in Bosnia "that artillery fire would be brought to bear on the city in response." Harland described a kind of tit for tat shelling that it -- with a heavy ratio of disproportionality, so the ration of 5:1, 10:1 or even more. And that's described in a report at -- by Harland and others which is captured in P896, a report of 2 July 1995 beginning: "The Serbs have responded by resuming a fairly indiscriminate bombardment of the down-town area and by increased sniper activity." And then he relates the killing of people in apartment building and the destruction of apartments on three floors and the condemnation by UNPROFOR of what it called highly inaccurate indiscriminate, highly destructive weapons of terror. General Wilson -- let me -- it brings to mind something specific that the accused said is that the Prosecution hadn't -- hasn't -- has failed to prove that the Serbs would fire first without any provocation or without any context to defence. That is an illuminating comment because it appears to reflect the accused's view that any response is appropriate once there has been action by the other side and it entirely misses the point. The question is the nature of the response. And as you heard from the internationals, including, General Wilson, there was a vastly disproportionate response. As he said, so ti's important to understand that while provocative conduct had been perhaps perpetrated by one side, the response was entirely disproportionate to the threat engendered by this activity. And he described as typical a situation where two or three rounds would be fired by mortar and approximately 200 rounds were fired in response distributed over a wide area full of apartment buildings, many of which were hit and set alight. And he stated the obvious that it was: "Entirely disproportionate to respond to two rounds in this manner that can cause so much damage and so much collateral damage." And General Rose said the same thing, the usual response from the -- by the way, for Wilson that cite is -- you can look T3949 through 3951. And 4131 through 4133, Rose said the same that was their method of responding because they didn't have the same level of infantry. And he referred to these attacks as disproportionate. And they included direct, punitive attacks on civilians, as the evidence reveals, intended to punish the population of Sarajevo as a whole. The collective punishment of the people of Sarajevo in addition to their -- to the leveraging of that population as a means to extract concessions or gain. Mr. President, I note the time. I want to continue with Counts 9 and 10 when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we recessed, I was addressing the accused's submissions concerning indiscriminate fire, militarily unjustified actions, Sarajevo as a civilian zone, and civilians as targets of Bosnian Serb military action. I had just addressed a point dealing with, in part, collective punishment of the civilians, and I wanted to turn next to direct the Court's attention to one of the -- some of the pieces of evidence concerning an aspect of the terror campaign that addresses both the terror inflicted on the civilian population and the nature of the weaponry used in the absence of military justification. And that's the use of modified air bombs. Quite simply, these weapons can't be directed at a selected target with any reasonable degree of precision. They are improvised bombs which are: "Highly inaccurate and particularly destructive." See, for example, P1953, paragraph 42. Konings explained to the Court that modified air bombs could destroy a complete block of offices and had a 50 to 60 metre radius of destruction. P1953, para 42. Enormously destructive weapons. Military witnesses, such as Overgard, P2058; Fraser, P1762; Brennskag, P1851, could not conceive of a battle-field situation in which this sort of bomb would be considered an appropriate weapon because one never knew where and when it would explode. But, as Konings explained: "Accurate targeting didn't matter in Sarajevo." The fact that they - that is, the modified air bombs - hit an office building -- another -- another office -- an office building, excuse me, was: "...pure luck. It could have hit a church, or an apartment block, or another office building. It didn't matter where it hit. Sometimes it frightened people, and sometimes it killed people. Every single round the Serb forces fired into the city, frightened people, and that's what we wanted, to frighten people." P1953, para 43. And in a similar way, the sniping in Sarajevo was also an organised centralised effort to target the civilian population but with a different mechanism. So as Banbury explained to the Court: "There was no reason for the Serbs to be sniping in Sarajevo. There were no military targets suitable for sniping. The argument that the military, including off-duty soldiers, were intermingled with the population and that therefore sniping was justified ..." Said Banbury: "... is belied by the fact that civilians, including women, children, and the elderly, were regularly victims of sniping." That's P2451, para 32. And he explained that: "The preponderance of victims of sniping in Sarajevo were civilians. And sniping is not an indiscriminate weapon the way, say, mortars are." I'm quoting Banbury here. "... mortars are somewhat indiscriminate. Sniping is very targeted at a single individual, and the victims of sniping that UNPROFOR was concerned with, and the people who were routinely victims in Sarajevo, were civilians." That's transcript 13317 through 13318. As Harland noted: "When a civilian was killed by sniping, it cannot be attributed as collateral damage." P820, para 300. The deliberate nature of the targeting of civilians through sniping is underscored by the fact that Bosnian Serb snipers targeted civilians who were engaged in clearly civilian activities, such as riding bicycles, collecting water, or riding on trams. And see P896, KDZ090, P2923, P1762, page 39, P1638, para 183. The psychological impact of sniping and its intended impact was described by sniping expert, Patrick van der Weijden: "A victim killed by a sniper only affects the victim and the people in the direct vicinity, but the thought of never being safe from the enemy affects everybody. Apart from being shot at, the anxiety mainly comes from not knowing where or exactly when the sniper will strike." P1620, page 8. And as General Fraser explained trams become a "favourite target" of the snipers because of the psychological impact it had on the people of the city. P1762, page 39. And in connection with these arguments by the accused, let me also mention the inter-relationship in this context of the deprivation of utilities because that -- those restrictions not only directly increased the suffering of the civilian population and heightened the terror but it also, as I alluded to a moment ago, made them more vulnerable to attack. So as the Bosnian Serb side deprived the city of utilities and humanitarian supplies, civilians, who then became targets, were forced to go outside to collect food and water. As Harland explained: "The Serbs would often shell places where people gathered for water because people had to gather there in larger numbers. When they were not lining up for water or food, people were normally hiding in their apartments or in their cellars and would therefore be less vulnerable to sniping and shelling." P820, paragraph 198. As we saw from P829, page 1 through 3, a weekly Sector Sarajevo report from June of 1995: "Civilians have been killed at water lines and market places. Negotiations to restore utilities are being blocked by the Serb military. UNHCR has brought in a small amount of food during the week, but next week's convoys have been cancelled by the Serbs following an incident in which the Bosnians shelled a convoy." Further on, the report provides additional details: "Serb gunners have a killed large number of Bosnian civilians this week, shelling water lines and market places. Seven people were killed and 12 injured while queueing for water in Dobrinja on Sunday, 18 June. On Wednesday, 21 June, six people were killed and 15 injured in another attack on a Dobrinja water line. The same day, five people were injured when a shell hit the Civljane outdoor market." Now, on Monday, the accused attempted to suggest that, notwithstanding this overwhelming body of evidence, there was no motive for him and for the Bosnian Serb forces to terrorise Sarajevo. You can find that at 28611. Actually, he asked the question rhetorically: What would have been the motive for us to terrorise Sarajevo? And the evidence in this case provided a very powerful answer in the form of evidence from a large number of witnesses. And that is that terrorising the city gave the Bosnian Serbs political leverage that they would not otherwise have had. As large numbers of international observers concluded, collectively Sarajevo was basically held at gunpoint, threatened, and abused for 44 months to mete out punishment and extract concessions from the Bosnian government. As General Rose explained, the shelling, sniping, and blockade of the city was: "... clearly to put pressure on the Bosnian government to bring about a peace deal on the Bosnian Serb terms." That's transcript 7271 through 7272. Harland identified this point in the context of shelling that, in his words: "... had no identifiable military tactical purpose but seemed intended to keep the civilian population of Sarajevo locked down, vulnerable, fearful, isolated." P820, para 33. And, indeed, the timing and intensity of the attacks and the deprivations reflected that strategy. Harland explained that the accused would modulate the terror, increasing attacks on civilians in order to influence negotiations and then periodically reducing attacks in order to avoid any western military intervention. "The overall strategy of Karadzic, having obtained 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina, seemed to be try to modulate the level of suffering in Sarajevo, to increase it, to encourage the Bosnians to accept Serb peace, or to reduce it in the face of threats of western military intervention, such as NATO air-strikes." P820, para 36. As KDZ450 noted, there was no strategy to concur the town but a strategy to exert pressure on the authorities and the population. Bell told this Court: "By tightening the grip on the city economically and militarily, the Serb thoughts they could effect a peace deal favourable to themselves." P1996, para 60. And he described it as a "noose around the neck of the people" which could be tightened or loosened. And this form of collective punishment in response to -- was -- was undertaken in response, as you've heard, to Bosnian military offensives or sometimes in pure retribution for that. So either to publish collectively or to make the Bosnian government think twice about whether to undertake further offensives. And Banbury heard this from Mladic himself, who acknowledged that the VRS would target civilians: "... to punish the Bosnian government authorities for actions elsewhere. It was retaliation for something that was happening elsewhere. They were using sniping as a tool, a point of leverage, a way to punish." That's T13330 and 13331. So, as an example, following the Bosnian Serbs' loss of the Marshal Tito barracks, van Lynden witnessed: "... wild scattered shelling across the city." Which he said: "... could only have been an expression of anger or was meant to punish and frighten the population." That's P926, para 56. Now, the accused suggested on Monday that the Bosnian Serb forces under his control practiced only a policy of "containment." Now, that assertion misrepresents both the -- and it was his contention that this was the position of the UN witnesses who testified here. But that submission by the accused misrepresents both the quantity and, indeed, the content of the testimony to which he alluded. UNMO Richard Mole was the only UN witness to refer to a containment strategy, and he explained what he meant and made it clear that it did not preclude pressure, coercion, and terror. He explained: "The Serbs risked more to trying to take Sarajevo militarily than the possible advantages gained by doing so. The position they were already in allowed them to achieve their political gains. They could do so by applying pressure to the city to achieve their aims elsewhere. If they took the city militarily, they removed a pressure point which could be used politically." And that's at P1426, para 36. And this observation, contrary to the accused's submission, tracks the conclusions of other international observers. So when Major Thomas arrived Sarajevo in October of 1993, he received an order of battle advising him that in Sarajevo: "The primary aim of the Bosnian Serb army is political. Their intent is to put pressure on the Presidency to come to a political settlement to end the war. The secondary aim is to fix Bosnian forces in Sarajevo so that they cannot threaten the Bosnian Serb army forces or be used in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's P1568, page 5. So whatever military benefit the Bosnian Serb forces and the Bosnian Serb leadership received by encircling the city, it was distinct from their wide-spread and organised campaign of violence against civilians which international witness after international witness recognised as a means of leveraging, attempting to leverage concessions or to collectively punish the population with bombs, bullets, and deprivations. Now, the accused also asserted on Monday that no incident has been proved, and he did that in the context of a flurry of submissions, but basically the submission was no incident was proved as having been committed by the Serb side, either sniping or shelling. So let me as quickly as possible just try to address that with a couple of examples. First of all, this, as we know, the Trial Chamber has already taken judicial notice of facts that show generally and that were buttressed over and over and over again by the testimony of internationals that civilians in Bosnian-held areas of Sarajevo were frequently targeted by gun-fire from SRK-controlled forces and areas of Grbavica, Ozrenska, Spicasta Stijena, Sirokaca, et cetera. And those are adjudicated facts 69, 70, 81, 121, 123, 124, 76, 77, and so on. And has taken judicial notice of what it heard of over and over again during the course of the case, too, that civilians were targeted during funerals, in ambulances, in hospitals, in trams, when driving, or cycling, at home, or fetching water. That's adjudicated facts 111 through 114. It's taken judicial notice of the fact that children were targeted. Adjudicated facts 115 to 910. And specific areas throughout Sarajevo became notorious as sources of sniping fire against civilians. Adjudicated fact 120. Including the Jewish cemetery, the Orthodox church, the school for the blind in Nedzarici, and so on. See adjudicated fact 125. And against that backdrop, the Trial Chamber has taken judicial notice of specific other incidents and heard considerable evidence about those. Let me just focus on, if I may, two specific sniping incidents, and then I will move onto quickly discuss shelling, I hope. Two examples, F15. And that involves a public tram that was shot on the 27th of February, 1995, leaving 30 bullet-holes and marks on the left side of the tram. That's adjudicated fact 2983. The Court will recall that among the victims of that attack wer Alma Mulaosmanovic-Cehajic and Alija Holjan [phoen]. That's adjudicated fact 2979. Origin of fire was from high-rise buildings in Grbavica. Shots were fired by a member of the SRK. See 2984. Those facts are more than sufficient, of course, to establish deliberate targeting of civilians by SRK forces, but the Prosecution has supplemented and corroborated those facts with a range of investigative expert and eye-witness evidence, confirming that the incident location was exposed to a direct and clear line of fire from those high-rise apartments, the ones that were notorious SRK sniping positions, and from which the civilian population in the area was regularly targeted. That is P492, page 10. In April of 1996 local investigators entered apartments in each of those buildings and found numerous apartments above the tenth floor that had been converted into sniper locations. T7933. Photographs documenting the unobstructed sight-lines from the gun holes in those apartments show that at least eight of those sniper positions were trained on the location of the incident, F15. That's P1738. Or similarly, F9. So the Chamber has already found that on the early evening of the 26th of June, 1994, teenagers - that's Senela Muratovic and Medina Omerovic - were walking to Omerovic's apartment on what was then Djure Jaksica Street when Muratovic was hit by a single sniper shot to her right shoulder, fired from the area of the school for the blind in a known sniping, SRK sniping location, as I mentioned. You can see adjudicated fact 222, 228, 224, 226, and Exhibit P2207. The distance between the origin of fire and the position of the victim was about 200 metres, see 232; no fighting was ongoing, see 229; a Muratovic, a civilian, was deliberately targeted from SRK controlled territory, 22 -- 233. And, again, while those facts are more than sufficient to establish the deliberate targeting. Again, the Prosecution have supplemented and corroborated those facts with the evidence which includes the UNMO daily sitrep, that's P1600, which reports that a few days after F9, on July 11, a 17-year-old boy had been wounded by sniper fire near the house for blind people, specifying that there had been three sniping incidents all involving civilians in the same spot in the last few days and that they suspected that the SRK was responsible for them. And then P1601 is an UNMO command daily sitrep from the 13th of July, 1994, reporting that the SRK commander of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade admitted to UNMO that SRK had been sniping from the house for blind people. Again, that's Exhibit P1601. And let me turn to shelling. Same generalised allegation by the accused. In that connection I would like to remind the Court of the adjudicated facts relating to G10 on April 7th, 1995, where a modified air boom fell and destroyed the house of Ziba Subo in Hrasnica - that's 3034 though 303 -- and 3037 - killing civilian and injuring others - 3038 - with extensive destruction in the area, including the destruction of their homes. See also 3040 indicating the area from which the air bomb was fired an area controlled by a SRK. The day before the incident, as we see in Exhibit P1201, SRK commander Dragomir Milosevic ordered the Ilidza Brigade to prepare a launcher with an air bomb and transport the bomb for launching, and to select the most profitable target in Hrasnice or Sokolovic Kolonija where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted. And the day of the incident, 7 April 1995, the SRK's daily report to the VRS Main Staff by Milosevic reported that their forces had responded to enemy fire by, among other things, launching a 250 kilogram air bomb at the centre of Hrasnica. You heard from Thorbjorn Overgard about what he saw when he arrived at the site: "We found the house totally demolished. There was nothing, not a brick standing nearby. One of the [indiscernible] nearly. Overgard, P2058, pages 15 through 17, and you saw the extent of the damage at P465, and in addition in Martin Bell's report at P2041. Now part of the accused's contention was that the Prosecution didn't prove that the Serbs fired more than the Muslims or that the Prosecution didn't prove that the Serbs fired first. Well, let me address those quickly. First of all, with respect to the first assertion, Konings estimated that mortar and artillery fire in Sarajevo was overwhelmingly of Serb origin, perhaps 100:1, P1953, page 12. And with respect to the latter contention I dealt with that to some extent earlier, noting the -- the nature of the accused's assertion that the focus should be on whether or not a shell or mortar or bullet was fired before the -- his forces fired and indicating that that misplaces the focus because the focus needs to be, as we heard from General Wilson and others, on the nature of the return fire, whether it was indiscriminate, disproportionate, punitive, and so on. But let me respond to that claim on its face that there's no proof that Serbs fired first with just two examples: G7 and G6. So in G7, that's an incident that occurred on the 4th of February, 1994. Three, 120-millimetre mortar shells struck a residential building in Dobrinja. And those shells killed at least eight civilians, including a child, and injured at least 22 people, including, two children. One shell hit a concrete wall in the backyard of an apartment, another impacted in the area of a playground, another hit a window frame on the ground floor apartment. There were more than 100 civilians in an open area near the parking garage, mostly children, when the shelling took place. Some of the victims were cueing for humanitarian aid. That's P156. There were no military units or military personnel where the humanitarian aid was being unloaded or close to these sites. That's AF 318 though 319, 323. A detailed investigation was undertaken of the two impacts that resulted in the civilian casualties. This -- if you see AF 320 you can see that the origin of fire was SRK held territory and we heard evidence they were fired from the Energoinvest complex of buildings which was controlled by the SRK.
