Not only were these civilians engaged in peaceful activities, but as you heard from Witness KDZ450, he specifically cited this as an example of Serbs opening fire on Bosnian Muslim territory without being provoked by the Bosnian forces. He specified: "Dobrinja was not a military target and it only led to civilian death, especially children." That's KDZ450 at transcript 10618. And similarly, G6 that's 22nd of January, 1994, two 82-millimetre mortar shells and one, 120-millimetre mortar shelled into the residential neighbourhood of Alipasino Polje, this time killing six children and greatly wounding three additional children and one adult civilian. Now, at the time of the shelling, there were two groups of children playing in the street and soon after the first mortar strike, two shells exploded near the entrances to nearby apartment buildings killing many of the children who were running to take cover after the initial explosion. These are adjudicated facts 283, 286, 287, and 292. Now, this attack took place on an otherwise quiet day during a lull in hostilities, no activity of a military nature was underway. There were no soldiers to be seen in the vicinity. That's adjudicated facts 298 and 299. Indeed, KDZ477 recalled that: "For an a number of days there hadn't been any shelling, so I know this was sudden. I think that the children went out to the play in the snow because there had not been any shelling, not only there but also in the broader area. Otherwise they wouldn't have been outside." That's at transcript 10923. Now this Trial Chamber has also received documentary evidence such as the UNMO report of military activity which states that: "An artillery barrage broke a period of relative quiet in the city, killing six children and critically injuring at least three others as they played together in the snow." P1700. Based on extensively analysis and testimony from local and UN investigators as well ballistics expert -- was established during the Galic trial and accepted as adjudicated fact in this trial that the impact traces from the shells were elliptical and considerably more pronounced to the west leading to the conclusion as accepted here as well that the three shells were fired from SRK positions to the west of Alipasino Polje and originating from SRK territory and forces. Again, two incidents which directly belie a conclusion which in and of itself indicates or was a predicate to the retaliatory and collective punishment fire of the Bosnian Serb forces. On Monday the accused also indicated that the Prosecution did not prove that he had a negative attitude towards civilian matters or the welfare of civilians, and there had been no interference with humanitarian aid or humanitarian efforts in order to contribute to the suffering of civilians. That assertion is belied by the weight of the evidence and directly contradicted by it, as with the other submissions. So Banbury, for example, explained that: "As Karadzic constantly demonstrated he could open or close, in this case the airport, whenever he wished." And that this power: "Provided particularly powerfully leverage to the Bosnian Serb leadership." That's P2451, paragraph 65 and 211. And he gave evidence of the specific example in which the accused closed the airport, refused to open it while the Bosnian Serbs were under sanctions and threatened to impose additional restrictions. That's P2451, paragraphs 143 through 145. There's related comment in connection with that, where the accused suggested that all aid received by the population of Sarajevo was -- resulted from his beneficence and any drop of water, I think he referred to, they were response for, and the Prosecution did not show efforts to sabotage the civilian life in Sarajevo. Again, that is contradicted by the evidence from observers who were present and dealt directly with the accused and his forces. So on the 20th of September, 1994, for example, in meetings involving General Rose and David Harland, in the context of a Bosnian attack out of Sarajevo two days earlier, the accused threatened to "flatten the Presidency," unquote, "if there were a repetition of the episode," unquote. He also expressed his concern that the Security Council would tighten sanctions on the RS and said this would put UNPROFOR in the position of having sided with the enemy. In his words, that is, the accused's words: "If the international community treats us like a beast then we will behave like a beast." He specifically mentioned in this regard "the use of utilities as a means of war." And that's P834, page 1 through 2. As General Rose explained, the Serbs responded to the assaults of the Bosnian army by cutting off the electricity and gas and halting the flow of commercial goods and aid convoys to Sarajevo. That's P1638, para 118. Mr. President, as before, I may return to some aspects of Counts 9 and 10, but in order not to intrude improperly, my view on our submissions related to other counts, I want to move to the counts related to Srebrenica. Your Honours, during the Prosecution's opening statement, we explained some of the evidence that would be introduced regarding the accused's responsibility for Count 2 and the other Srebrenica-related counts of the case. And as you have seen and as the evidence shows, those assertions are wholly supported by the evidence in this case. So, for example, I spoke about the fact that the accused ordered the operation to take Srebrenica which was a culmination of his efforts to cleanse Eastern Bosnia. The evidence shows that to be the case. P02276, the 9 July VRS Main Staff order; P1412, at page 111; P1415, at pages 84 and 86. The evidence also shows that he was informed of the progress of the operation throughout the course of the operation by various means. Including from General Mladic himself, from VRS reports, from MUP reports, from state security reports. And see the testimony of Richard Butler, of 17 April 2012, T27473 through 27474, explaining that the accused received information from three chains. The VRS, the MUP, and state security. The evidence shows that the accused had direct contact with Mladic, maintained direct contact also with his hand selected civilian commissioner for the area. And for that, see P04911, page 48; P04556, page 35 - it's Prmovic [phoen] and Ristic; D0205, the 11 July presidential directive appointing Deronjic the military civilian commissioner; P4374, the Katanic amalgamated statement at paragraph 70 stating that Deronjic had daily telephone contact with Karadzic. The evidence demonstrates that the accused knew that the population was being moved out as it was happening - that's P4464, 13 July VRS Main Staff report - that he ordered the removal of men, that is the Muslim prisoners, from an area where there was a risk they would be seen by the internationals. That's P4618, the intercept of 13 July with Deronjic. See also the Butler testimony at T27557 through 27560 stating that international convoys were waiting to enter Bratunac on 13 July. And the evidence supports the -- that the accused knew that men were being killed. In that regard, see P02242, the accused's agenda entry of 14 July 1991 about his meeting with Deronjic; see P4382, the 14 July video SRT news report of the meeting with Deronjic; see P304374, paragraph 70, about the accused's daily telephone contact with Deronjic; P4374, paragraph 72, that's Katanic stating that he believed Deronjic had indeed reported the killings to the accused. See his testimony at T24466.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tieger kindly slow down a little for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just referring to the testimony found at transcript page 24466, stating that Karadzic was a Deronjic superior. See his testimony at 24474, stating that on 13 July Deronjic told Katanic about the killings. And see closed session testimony at 24224, to 24225 about an order that Deronjic gave on the 13th of July to load the bodies at Kravica and that he later gave the order to dig the grave at Glogova. And the evidence demonstrates, as we asserted in the opening, that the accused covered up the mass expulsions and the murders and indeed continues to do so to this very day. See P04359, that's the "El Pais" interview where the accused denies any crime; P05235, that's the 17 July David Frost interview where the accused states there are no missing men; the Erdemovic testimony on 27th of February, 2012, T25356 and 25357; and see P3163, e-court page 6, an order issued by the accused on 23rd of March, 1996: "The Republika Srpska Army Main Staff and the Ministry of Interior shall immediately form a mixed expert commission to fully investigate and determine the facts regarding the alleged discovery of two decomposed bodies at the scene of earlier battles with the Muslim side in the Pilica area in the Zvornik municipality." And, of course, as we asserted in the opening and as you've seen in the evidence, his expression of regret about the operation was only that some of the Muslims had gotten away, and, for that, see the 52nd Session -- the 52nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on 6th of August, 1995, pages 23 through 24. And it is against that backdrop and a great deal of other evidence that I will address some of the specific assertions, some of the misrepresentations made by the accused on Monday. At transcript 28588 on Monday, the accused claimed that it was proven: "Beyond any doubt that the Serbian army did not have contact with the population in Srebrenica, did not have any combat contact with the 28th division, did not have any contact with the population for this contact occurred in Potocari." Now, this assertion, as others, is simply false, patently false indeed. Just to give one example, we have clear evidence in the record that the VRS and specifically the 10th Sabotage Detachment, which as you know was a unit directly attached to the VRS Main Staff, did indeed have contact with some elderly people as well as able bodied Muslim men who surrendered to them in the centre of Srebrenica. And it's instructed that not only is it untrue that they didn't have any contact but the nature of the contact is significant. And to see the nature of the contact, we can turn to e-court -- turn to P4202, page 55 in e-court. On the express order of their commander, Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis, they slit the Muslim man's throat and left his body lying in the centre of square of Srebrenica in front of a bank across the square from the mosque. You can see his blood flowing down the street. Erdemovic testified about that. You can also find that at P332 and at T10946, 10947. And he said: "He came out," that's this man we see on screen, "surrendered and said that he was not in the army. They had no problem with the Serbs, had nothing against Serbs, something like that, I can't remember exactly the words." Erdemovic testified that there was no fierce fighting at the time and VRS soldiers began to mistreat the man and that: "Not long after that Pelemis ordered a Vlasenica Platoon member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment to slit the man's throat. And he was executed immediately in that manner." So, there is indeed evidence of contact, and in this case, contact between an elite unit of the Serbian army and the population in Srebrenica before the events in Potocari. A single piece of evidence among others that repulse or rebuts the accused's assertion that murder didn't occur where the military or the MUP had a strong presence or that -- in that -- he made that assertion at 28591, or that commanders didn't know about murders. That's an assertion at 28594, and that there was no intent to forcibly remove the population of Srebrenica. That's -- he said that at 28588. The accused also claimed that: "Silence reined everywhere with regard to the mass executions after the fall of Srebrenica." A suggestion that people didn't know and certainly he couldn't know what was going on. To the contrary, the Prosecution has shown that in his role as RS president and supreme commander of the RS forces, the accused was constantly kept abreast of developments on the ground and knew about the actions and direct implications of those actions of his forces in the murder operation at the time of the events. Now he asked sort of rhetorically, How could the president of the republic possibly know? And here are some of the evidence in response. First of all, as expert witness Butler indicated, the murder operation was organised and implemented like any other military operation. The same military bureaucracy and flow of information: "The same process and procedures of the Drina Corps, the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade for the most part would use as part of their everyday military operations were also followed for their role on the conduct of the crimes. The military chain of command in that regard worked as it's supposed to." That's at type T27635. The VRS and MUP reports were directed to President Karadzic. P02276, P3054, P4464, P4457, P5137. These reports clearly indicate that he was kept abreast of the development of the operations on the ground. He regularly met with civilian, military, and MUP authorities. For example, he met on the 13th, the 14th, the 15th, and the 18th of July with deputy minister of interior Kovac who, in turn, received daily reports of the development of the operation on the ground. And for that, see P2242, e-court page -- pages 91 through 93. Now, two examples of the accused's direct knowledge include this -- these. On 14th of July, there's a very urgent VRS Main Staff daily report directed to the RS president. P4457. And it reported to the accused that VRS forces were "scouring the terrain and receiving a large number of Muslim fugitives who are surrendering to them." Another, D02002. On the 16th of July at 1615 hours, the Main Staff reported to Mladic that the accused had called because he had been informed that Pandurevic had arranged for the Muslim's safe passage over their territory. In other words, as soon as the accused was informed that Pandurevic had opened the corridor in contravention of the order to destroy the Muslim column, Karadzic called the Main Staff to further inquire about it. Now, the accused also suggested -- or in the course of these submissions suggested that the people in the chain of command did not know what was happening. I'm going to point to just one piece of testimony that contradicts that powerfully, but I need to go into private session to do so. And that's going to be a piece of testimony that indicates clearly that the VRS chain of command knew of the order to kill the prisoners in Zvornik. So if we could go to -- into private session, I'd like to read what was said about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, in this connection, let me just mention the accused's contacts with Miroslav Deronjic, the man he appointed the civilian commissioner of the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica the very same day that the Serbian forces took over the enclave. That's D02055. And I might mention parenthetically that in chronological terms this is far from the first time that the Court has heard reference to Deronjic's role in the efforts of the Bosnian Serb forces and authorities to secure territory in Eastern Bosnia. You will recall his role in the cleansing of the Bratunac municipality in 1992. Now we see him personally appointed by the accused as the civilian commission of the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica. But in that connection, I want to look at the critical time of the 13th and 14th of July. We know as I've stated earlier that on the evening of the 13th Deronjic was well aware of the Kravica massacre and was busy covering it up. In particular, on the evening of the 13th, he ordered that a mass grave be dug in Glogova for those killed at Kravica. You will find that in closed testimony at T24224 through 227. On that very evening, the accused and Deronjic discussed the issue of prisoners over the phone. That's P04618. The morning after, on July 14th, while the prisoners were still being transported to the Zvornik area, the accused personally met Deronjic. That's P2242, e-court page 91, and also P04382. These circumstances, given the nature of the timing, the nature of the role of the respective parties, the nature of their long-standing connection are more than sufficient by themselves to show beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused was informed about the murder operation. Now, the accused has also argued that directive 7.1, does not contain the language that can be found in directive 7. And that in that connection, humanitarian aid did not cease, and that indeed, he asserts that convoys "ceaselessly travelled," and that the children in Srebrenica were well nourished and healthy. Let me address both of these claims since they are all connected. First of all, the evidence has shown clearly that directive 7.1 did not supplant, replace, or in any way negate directive 7. As explained by military expert Butler: "What directive 7.1 represents is a technical expansions of the goals of directive 7 more designed for military planners." That's T27450, lines 11 through 17. Now, the evidence shows and the Prosecution has shown that, consistent with directive 7, convoys were indeed let through sporadically and that complies with and follows through on the orders given in directive 7, which is P838: "Through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits. Reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population making them dependant on our goodwill, while, at the same time, avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Indeed specifically referring to the section on the Drina Corps in directive 7, that is, the section that reads, in part: "By planned and well thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." General Milovanovic testified that this task was assigned to the Drina Corps directly by the Supreme Command. That's T25504, lines 23 through 24. And P4481, Krivaja 95, the Drina Corps plan to attack Srebrenica refers to directive 7 and 7.1, showing that directive 7 didn't supplant or replace directive 7. And beyond that, the accused himself stated that Krstic planted the Srebrenica operation in front of him. That's at interview P4555 and P5121, and indeed while watching the television coverage on July 14th, 1995, the accused bragged to Witness Djordjevic that the attack on Srebrenica was part of "my order number 7." And that it was intended to bring "the temperature to the boiling point." That's T25906 through 25908, also see P4515 at e-court page 12. And the evidence has shown that the humanitarian situation in the enclave, due to the restriction on humanitarian aid, a restriction in accordance with directive 7 was particularly dire. Resulting in a lack of food for the Muslim civilians in the enclave, these convoy restrictions can be linked directly to the accused, as the evidence shows that the accused was directly involved in the issuance of convoy permits. You can see that, for example, in P4543, his decision on forming a state committee for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations. This decision of 14 March 1995 only a few days after the issuance of directive 7 makes clear that permits for the movement of convoys shall be issued by the co-ordinating body pursuant to the state committee's decision. That's Article 6. Now, these restrictions also strangle DutchBat who with their -- who received their last fuel supply in February of 1995. You heard the testimony of Momir Nikolic that the problems with the supply of DutchBat intensified during the period between March or April and the fall of Srebrenica. So between those two periods of time. And that's T24573. And, as a result, DutchBat was unable to do its job because of the lack of logistical support, just as directive 7 had ordered and envisioned. Now, the accused also argued on Monday that the Muslim population left voluntarily and that the "evacuation" was favoured by the authorities. That's -- he said that at T28588. This is a submission which is contrary to voluminous material received by the Trial Chamber. To the contrary, the clear intent to deport the population was readily apparent in a 1994 Bratunac Brigade order from Commander Ognjenovic who stated clearly that the goal was an "entirely Serbian Podrinje," and that: "The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." That's P4075. It's dated July 4th, 1994. And in considering this matter and the accused's submission, particular attention should be paid to the conditions, the desperate conditions that the accused and the VRS imposed on the enclave in order to make life unbearable in the months leading up to the attack which contributed to the population's lack of any choice but to leave. So let's look first at food supply and it's impact on the voluntariness of any decision to leave the enclave. As you've heard, one method by which the VRS and the accused ensured that the Muslim population was forced to leave was through lack of food. You heard from several DutchBat witnesses who testified about the lack of food in the enclave. And you no doubt recall Witness Rutten's photo of the DutchBat garbage dump where the Muslim population routinely gathered with the hopes of finding anything to eat. This lack of food, again, was directly linked to restrictions on humanitarian convoys, restrictions were ordered by the accused in directive 7. As to the accused's submission that even Prosecution witness Schmitz testified about seeing healthy children and that that was a sign of sufficient food, the Trial Chamber need only recall the testimony of Mirsada Malagic, a woman who lost her husband and two sons, and who told this Chamber about people who died of starvation and the fact that she herself nearly succumbed, and as she explained: Even if you're starving and your kids are hungry too, you sacrifice for them. T23467. And if there was food to be had, as Christine Schmitz told the Trial Chamber, people would only beg for it after dark because they felt ashamed. It is one reflection of the impact of the purposeful restriction of food supplies in order to ensure the departure of the Muslim population. Another was shelling. And you heard testimony about shelling. If there was any doubt about whether or not civilians were targeted, you could only -- you need only turn to the testimony of Colonel Kingori whose job, in part, was to monitor the shelling itself. He testified: "The way the shelling was done was definitely aimed at the residents of the place." That's P04140, at paragraph 73, e-court page 17. Finally, even if Muslims reached Potocari under those circumstances, the VRS ensured that they were presented with no option but to leave. Now, you heard witnesses describing the population as "totally exhausted, panicked, fearful, with death in their eyes." And while those people waited in Potocari, hoping to escape from the grasp of those who had starved and shelled them, General Mladic himself provided further confirmation of the real lack of choice that existed. In an intercept on 12th, he stated: "We will evacuate them all, those who want to leave, and those who do not." P4254. A few days later on the 16th of July, 1995, Zvornik Brigade Commander Pandurevic emphasised that the job was not done until all the Muslims had been forced out: "I consider that the Krivaja 95 operation is not complete as long as a single enemy soldier or civilian remains behind the front line." P00180. Turn to the accused's assertion at transcript page 28591 that there were no killings in Potocari. This is simply false. Both Scheduled Incidents for Potocari killings, that is, E14.1, the killing of nine men near the UN compound and E14.2, the killing of one man near the white house, have been proven by the evidence. And, again, one only need to look at the testimony of Rutten and Groenewegen. Johannes Rutten stated at P3948, paragraph 70, the following". "As we got into the meadow, we saw that the men were shot down. I inspected all the men that were on the ground. They were all civilian men, at least they had civilian clothes on. There were nine of them. They were lying with their faces toward the stream. Two were lying on their sides as if they had looked back. The rest of them were lying with their faces to the stream. They had all shots at their back at heart height. There were shots of small calibre weapons. The men were all about 45 to 55 years old. The blood was still running. There were no flies on them, and it was very warm that day so you could easily say that it had not been longing ago that they were shoot. The bodies were warm." And Paul Groenewegen at P4 -- 4167, paragraph 61: "I saw the soldiers placing the man with his face to the wall, and from a distance of about 3 metres, shoot him through the head. Just before that, my attention had already been attracted then as well by shouting and it was the same person that was concerned, and I recognised him the second time about 10 to 15 minutes past between me first seeing him and the execution. The man was wearing civilian clothes, blue jeans and a blue-green sweater. As far as I could see, he was not armed." And let me turn next to the accused's assertion that no killings took place before the Kravica executions. This is another assertion that is wrong. The Kravica warehouse killings were not the first. The executions at Jadar river took place on the 13th of July at sometime before noon. A Jadar river survivor testified about the executions - excuse me - and the timing which was sometime before noon on the 13th of July. See P00335. It's a public redacted version. See also adjudicated fact 1689. On the morning of 13 July, 16 Bosnian Muslim men who had been captured from the column were transported by bus from the warehouse in Konjevic Polje to the Jadar riverbank. Amongst them was a 15-year-old boy. And as a reminder and in connection with a suggestion made by the accused in regard to the timing of the events, the mass killings continued during and after the Kravica killings with the executions at Sandici meadow and later at Luka school, which further undercuts the accused's suggestion that the events were the results of chaos. You also heard that the accused's submission that no killings took place in areas where "there was a greater military or a police presence" or where state authorities were present or with the knowledge or approval of state authorities. And given the weight of the evidence, this submission is patently untrue, even absurd, and cannot have been intended for the Court that was -- or for those of us who were following the evidence in the case. The opposite is true. The mass executions were carried out in an organised manner by the VRS and MUP and under the noses of the hand-picked civilian authorities. I already spoke about Deronjic and the burial of the bodies of those murdered in Kravica, their burial in Glogova. KDZ320 was informed by Beara while prisoners who were still alive in Zvornik that they would be killed. And that the assistance of the local authorities was needed to bury the bodies. That's P4989, public redacted version, 4990 and transcript 7940 through 7945. The mass executions in Orahovac were carried out at least in part by Zvornik Brigade 4th Battalion soldiers, such as Gojko Simic. And you can look to P768, transcript 711 through 725, regarding the recognition of Simic, his death certificate indicating that he was a member of the 4th Battalion. That's P45 -- P4976. In Kozluk, it was the Zvornik Brigade 2nd Battalion and the Zvornik Brigade MPs and uniformed MUP members who were present. That's KDZ496. P386, or public redacted 387, transcript 32702. And you can see also in that connection KDZ105. The commander of the 2nd Battalion, P342, Dragan Jovic. KDZ257. 2nd Battalion driver for Sreco Acimovic, and you can see that at P364. Veljko Ivanovic. KDZ479, 2nd Battalion driver, P383. Next to the Pilica cultural hall at the time of the executions there was a check-point of the Republika Srpska civilian police. Can you see P332, transcript 10983 and transcript 10984. And the murders in Branjevo were carried out by the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the VRS Main Staff, the same unit which murdered the man in the very centre of Srebrenica whose picture we saw a bit earlier. Now, you can find evidence of the systematic nature of the operation and the presence of VRS -- VRS, MUP and civilian authority forces everywhere in various pieces of evidence as I've only touched upon. But nothing could be clearer regarding the widespread knowledge and participation of the VRS and MUP and command levels than the statement I referred to in private session before. And in that regard, if I could return to private session to amplify on that just a bit and further underscore the weight of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally I'd like to conclude with respect to Count 2 and the related counts in connection with the events in Srebrenica by focussing very briefly on the accused's argument that there was no intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica. Your Honours to the contrary, the evidence demonstrates that the crimes, murder, cruel and inhumane treatment by terrorising and beating in Potocari and beating before execution, all of these crimes were perpetrated with genocidal intent. Let me point to just to some of the evidence. The scale and nature of the operation, the systematic and organised manner in which it was carried out, the methodical attempt to eliminate every single Bosnian Muslim male of Srebrenica other than some children and a few elderly men. The accused himself alluded to the number of victims. The number of victims the Prosecution has established that at least 6.772 Bosnian Muslim men were killed by Bosnian Serb forces under the command of the accused in the execution of this plan, this genocidal plan. All of this can only be explained by the clear intention to destroy the group as such. On the 6th of August, when the international media and organisations became fully aware of mass executions, or at least had sufficient knowledge of what had happened to be desperately seeking explanations, and the matter was alive in the media, and in international and political circles, the accused addressed events in Srebrenica. He expressed some regret but not for the crime. He regretted that some 9.000 men had survived, that General Krstic could not finish it all. Your Honours, these are merely some of the pieces of evidence, and that -- that's -- by the way, that's P1412. Those are merely some of the pieces of evidence indicating that genocide was committed by the Bosnian Serb forces in Srebrenica and that the accused, the supreme commander of these forces, was engaged in his role with the intent required by the Statute and the elements of genocide, the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims in whole or in part, as such. Mr. President, I would be moving on to another portion of our submissions. I think, given the time, it's probably best to adjourn and resume after the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, as I indicated at the outset, I'd like to turn now to the book ends of the indictment, that's Counts 1 and 11, and first address this Defence submission with respect to Count 1. Those arguments, as will recall, were made by Mr. Robinson. He asked you, for example, to take the word of the ICJ that there was no genocide; that is, take their word for it, not his, I think, was the expression he used. Now, apart from the fact that this may not be quite sincere on its face, unless the accused wants you to take the ICJ's word for the fact that Srebrenica was genocide, it is this Trial Chamber that obviously has the responsibility to decide this case on the facts before it. Additionally, it may be worth noting that the factors cited by the Defence in connection with its submissions regarding the ICJ are not precisely apposite to this case; for example, he specifically cited the ICJ's discussion about the strategic goals and that it did not come to terms with the fact that an essential "motive" of much of the Bosnian Serb leadership to create a larger Serbian state by war or conquest, if necessary, did not necessarily require destruction of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat communities, but instead their expulsion. Now, as you know from our submissions, while we agree with the ICJ that the desire to create a Serbian state on the vast and ethnically intermixed territories sought by Dr. Karadzic required the expulsion of Muslims and Croats, the fact that the motive to have a Serb state could have been achieved in ways other than with the intent to commit genocide is not relevant. What is relevant is whether the dolus specialis existed irrespective of whether the underlying motive required it or, indeed, what that underlying motive was at all. Now the Defence also, in citing the figure of 2 per cent, asks you to play a numbers game and a numbers game that I think is a bit misleading as you will hear from other numbers that follow during the course of my submission with respect to particular municipalities; but more importantly, this citation as it was offered disregards the jurisprudence that makes clear that the size of the victimised population is not determinative, nor should it be. There's no minimum number of victims as the Stakic case said, that's, I believe, para 522: "It is not necessary to establish the size of the victimised community -- victimised population in numerical terms. It is the genocidal dolus specialus that predominantly constitutes the crime." And you can also look to the Trial Chamber in Semanza, which said: "There is no numeric threshold of victims necessary to establish genocide." The Defence also argues that displacement does not equal destruction but ignores the -- in so doing, ignores jurisprudence that displacement can contribute or be a part of the destruction or can be evidence of genocidal intent. And, finally, the Defence also cites the -- I shouldn't say finally, but the Defence also cites the Eichmann case, which shows, contrary to the Defence submission, that the existence of an intent to displace at one point in the process does not preclude genocidal intent at a later point. Now, the Defence also emphasised a number of earlier ICTY cases, including, Stakic, Brdjanin, Krajisnik, Milosevic, and Sikirica. Now, the -- the Sikirica and Jelisic, of course, differ factually from the other cases in so far as they do not appear to involved even local leadership figures or significant evidence outside the local camp focus. But, nevertheless, there was a discussion about Sikirica and an attempt to distinguish or at least emphasise a point in Sikirica as -- as being paralleled here. And that's the argument that in Sikirica there was no evidence that the killings were based on the targeting of the leadership. And the assertion was made well, that's -- that's the same here, for example, and the specific example of Koricanske Stijene was used. Mr. Robinson noted the culling out of men who fell into category C asserting that they were only combatants and that, therefore, evidence of targeting of the leadership did not exist in this case as it did not in Sikirica. Well, in fact, that is a mischaracterisation of the evidence. It is true that those -- that the evidence shows that those selected for execution at Koricanske Stijene fell under the category C, but as we heard in evidence, category C was not exclusively made up of combatants but, instead, included people who unmistakably would be identified as leadership figures, those who financed or gave more than simply verbal to their party, that is in contrast to category B, and -- or were members of other extremist organisation and party members, and so on. And that can be found, Your Honours, at P4257, pages T21119, and -- excuse me, 21119, and 21138 through 39, and I will return to the issue of leadership later. But the bottom line in the Defence submissions and one which they -- somewhat uncomfortably acknowledged but attempted to circumvent on the basis of reliance on a subsequent ICJ decision is that the Stakic Trial Chamber, the Brdjanin Trial Chamber, the Milosevic Trial Chamber, the Krajisnik Trial Chamber all concluded that, on the basis of the evidence before it, a reasonable Trial Chamber could, indeed, determine that the accused was legally responsible for genocide. Indeed, Mr. Robinson cited the Stakic Appeals Judgement but it was that Judgement which specifically noted that: "Without question, the Trial Chamber made factual findings which could, in principle, be taken as evidence that the Appellant intended to destroy the Bosnian Muslim group in part." And the Appellant Court found that on the basis of the evidence before it -- it did not conclude that the Trial Chamber was obliged to do so, but that it certainly could have done so. What the Trial Chamber in -- did find and that the Appeals Chamber alluded to was that: "The evidence presents a comprehensive picture of targeted killings, detentions, deportations and other violations of the basic rights of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in Prijedor, intended to bring about the destruction of the group as such, in part. The Trial Chamber finds at this stage of the procedure that a reasonable trier of fact could, on the basis of the evidence adduced in this case, be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that genocide was committed in Prijedor municipality in 1992." That's paragraph 35. And that is the case in the evidence before this Trial Chamber but, indeed, there is much more bearing on this particular accused's dolus specialus; evidence that demonstrates that he shared the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslim and/or Bosnian Croat groups in part and that he is therefore responsible for genocide under Count 1. And let me recite just some of that evidence. First of all, as we've seen repeatedly, and as I have eluded to earlier, the accused insisted that an independent Bosnia would result in the subjugation and genocide of the Bosnian Serbs by Muslims and Croats. And in the face of that perceived existential threat, he intended to use force that he knew and repeatedly claimed would physically destroy Bosnian Muslims and Croats. In the months leading up to the conflict, he threatened that Bosnian independence would result in the destruction of thousand of Muslims to the extent that the Muslim people would disappear. And when the Muslims and Croats, when those authority -- when their authorities did not yield to that threat but instead continued on the path toward independence, the forces and organs under the authority of the accused seized control of territories that he considered to be ethnically or historically Serb or to be strategically important, killing thousands of Bosnian Muslims and Croats and comitting other acts of genocide against thousands more. And these acts are exemplified in the municipalities listed in paragraph 38. The accused's statements both during and after the commission of these crimes demonstrate his approval and encouragement of these crimes as part of a process of "eliminating Bosnian Muslims and Croats." Now, I mentioned that the accused was obsessed with genocide and the Court will recall that the accused raised the World War II genocide of Serbs so frequently and routinely that Ambassador Okun actually noted down in his diary on one occasion when the accused had not mentioned it during the first three minutes of the conversation. That's at T1490 and P779, page 43. And what Ambassador Okun appreciated at the time and what we came to see in the evidence was that the boundaries of what the accused was prepared to do to the Muslim and Croat communities was measured by the existential threat he insisted they presented to Serbs. As Ambassador Okun said to the accused: "If you keep talking about the genocide of the Serbs so much, you will commit a pre-empted genocide." That's at T4165 of P776. And that -- that makes the obvious connection between the accused's fixation with the past genocide committed against the Serbs and his willingness to take actions as he deemed needed and appropriate under those circumstances to ward off a renewed threat of genocide that he believed the Bosnian Serbs faced. And these were not views that he kept to himself, as the pre-eminent leader of the Bosnian Serbs and supreme commander of its forces, he promulgated those views and espoused them among his followers. For example, he told the Assembly at its inaugural session on the 24th of October, 1991, that there was "nothing new" in the developments in Yugoslavia at the time: "We see the same uniforms, the same people who embraced fascist Germany back then, the same plans, the same villains and the same victims." That's D82, page 25. And similarly in January 1994 at a ceremonial session of the Assembly he declared: "The wars of 1914, 1941 and 1991, were and remain above all wars for the extermination of the Orthodox population," meaning the Serb population, "there were a lot of nationally unaware Muslims, even Muslims who in the ethnic sense declared themselves as Serbs, but they still participated in the genocide against the Serbs led exclusively by religious reasons." Now, unhappily these were not abstract, philosophical ruminations. To the contrary, the accused insisted that Muslims and Croats must not live with Serbs in order for Serbs to be safe and this belief was the foundation of his overall military strategy. So when he announced the strategic objectives to the Assembly, he framed the first objective, separation, as: "Separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to stay together in the same state." And he formulated and implemented military policies to achieve this. That is from the 16th Session at P956, page 9. Long before the conflict broke out, the accused acknowledged that the destruction, the physical destruction, of Muslims and Croats would be a means to achieve his goals. He repeatedly threatened the Bosnian Muslim and Croat groups with extinction if the circumstances, as he viewed them, required the use of force by the Bosnian Serbs. And let me recite some of those. On 9 September 1991 a conversation where he proposed saying to the Muslims, Man, you will disappear. You will be annihilate. Many of us will disappear but you will be annihilate. P3200, page 2. On September 22nd, 1991, in discussing his negotiations with Izetbegovic he said: "Bosnia and the Muslims will disappear if there's a war." That's P5975. And in particular during the course of a long and contentious assembly session -- joint assembly session in mid-October of 1991, the accused repeatedly stated that the Bosnian Muslims would be physically destroyed if they deigned to move forward in the manner that he threatened would result in their destruction. So on October 12th, 1991, he said to Gojko Djoko, quote -- the Bosnian Muslim people "will disappear. That people will disappear from the face of the earth if they -- if they insist now." That is D00279, pages 3 and then at pages 7 through 8. He talks about 300.00 Muslims dying up to their necks in blood. The accused actually raised this during the course of the case with Dr. Donia, explaining that he was giving the Muslims "several options." That's at T3497 through 3498. But the final option that he articulated to Djogo 1991, should the Muslim continue to insist on independence, was their disappearance from the face of the earth. As Donia said to him when the accused put that proposition about options to Donia: "You determine what is successful or what is acceptable for the options they can pursue and if they choose to pursue other options or don't comply with your conditions that there will be this war, conflagration that will result in their disappearance." And two more conversations of the same ilk from the same week to another interlocutor in the same day, in P5959, the accused said: "Therefore, the Muslims know what it is. It is hell in which six hundreds of thousands of them will disappear. They will disappear." And a few days later, as the Court is aware, he stood on the podium at the joint assembly, wagged his finger at the Muslims and Croats and told them that Bosnian independence would, quote, would entail, quote: "The same highway of hell and suffering" that Slovenia and Croatia went through and result in the "possible extinction of the Muslim people because," quote, "Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war here." That's D267, pages 3 through 4. And as events marched on toward the independence of Bosnia, the accused continued to insist that physical destruction awaited those who sought it. On the 31st of December, 1992, an interview was published with Izetbegovic in which he called for the establishment of a sovereign and independent Bosnia. That is adjudicated fact 962. And the next day, the accused spoke about that with Mr. Krajisnik and he said: "Now he is talking openly of a sovereign and independent Bosnia. Does he want someone to destroy Sarajevo? We will release our tigers and let them do their job." That is P5879, page 5. And as we know from other evidence the accused was a very key figure, in fact, the key figure in preparing the organs intended to achieve these goals well aware of their destructive potential. It was the accused who personally selected General Mladic to lead the VRS - that's P970, page 317 - and he tasked the VRS with implementing the goal of physical separation through military force. In selecting General Mladic, the accused chose a commander who shared his belief that Serbs faced genocide and annihilation at the hands of Muslims and Croats, and that forcible physical separation was necessary to deal with this threat. As Mladic said at the 16th Session, the Serbs were "creating an army which will protect our children from the concurring ambitions of Nazi mercenaries." That's P956, page 45. And he underscored the difficulties that might be faced in reconfiguring Bosnia's demographic, stating both the difficulty in "shifting" people and people from here to there, and the unfavorable demographics in certain Serb claimed territories. Again, P956, pages 36 through 37. In the 1992 directives that were issued to and distributed among the Bosnian Serb forces, General Mladic disseminated the message that they were waging an ethnic war to protect Serbs from genocide. Here are just few an examples: The VRS's task was to protect Serbian populations from genocide and extermination. That's D232; to fight for the physical survival of the Serbs in this territory, D593; P956, the fourth directive describes the conflict as a defensive war for our freedom and against the genocide of the Serbian people; in D593, Mladic characterised the Muslim side as a "fanatic adversary who will be merciless to us and our people." And so on. Indeed, even after Mladic had led the VRS in forcibly and dramatically altering Bosnia's demographics, reflection of which you saw in the ethnic map I showed at the outset, Mladic continued to warn that Serbs were still under threat from Muslims and Croats. And emphasised that the answer to the threat lay in their permanent elimination. In January 1994, he explained to the Assembly: "This is our historical chance to create a state, not any kind of state but an all Serbian state with as little enemies as possible, those who could be our potential enemies and raise against us again in a few years." And he warned about the Muslims and Croats who "are like this, represent a danger," and that the "enemy it determined to fight until the last one of us lives." In light of the threat posed, he stated: "My concern is not that they will create the state. My concern is to have them vanish completely." That's P1385, pages 47 through 49. This was the man whom the accused entrusted to realise his vision of an ethnically homogenous Serbian state freed of its enemies for once and for all. Now, the accused also encouraged or authorised the elimination of Muslims and Croats by the organs under his authority and control. So, for example, at the 17th Assembly Session in July 1992, and that at -- that's a period when the violence against Muslims and Croats was particularly intense, when thousands of Muslims were dying in or being killed in camps, such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Susica, after having been rounded up from their homes, when many others had already been killed or -- or fled in terrified fear. The accused stated there was "truth" in one assembly deputy statement that: "The Muslims have been planted to us as a people whose executioners we are to be." That's found at D92, page 41. And the accused then added: "This conflict was roused in order to eliminate the Muslims. They think that they are being nationally established, but, in fact, they are vanishing." Now, notwithstanding the sufferings caused by his policy, the accused continued to pursue his objective. In June 1993, in a televised interview, he stated that: "The Muslims will have no excuse whatever for continuing the war. Muslim people should know that right now is the most favourable moment for them to save themselves from disappearance and to create their own space." And through such statements -- and these statements are coming from the paramount, the pre-eminent leader of the Bosnian Serbs. I showed you in the opening a statement by an assembly deputy who said that five lines of Dr. Karadzic were enough to change the whole session. And that came into evidence, as did the other assembly sessions. These views fostered a general atmosphere among all levels of Bosnian Serb leadership which promoted the physical destruction of Bosnian Muslims and Croats. This is illustrated by some comments that I'll note. For example, at the 4th Assembly Session, there's a comment by at regional leader, Mr. Vukic, that the European Community's recognition of an independent Bosnia would result in: "... another Serbian uprising, and there will be massive bloodshed, in which some nations that have been subsequently created as an illusion to the Muslims, will disappear all together." A comment that was met with applause as reflected in the transcript of the session. That's D86, page 27. At the 16th Assembly Session, the accused's minister of health, Dragan Kalinic stated: "Knowing who our enemy is, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically militarily destroyed and crushed which, of course, implies eliminating and liquidating their key people." And that harkens back to the issue about Koricanske Stijene and the categorising of local leaders for destruction. I might also note that -- that can be found at P956, page 17. If you turn to page 19 of the same session, you'll see the same speaker, Dr. Kalinic, urging the destruction of the Kosova hospital so that the enemy will have nowhere to go for medical help. That's the minister of health. And, in fact, key people among the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat groups were being eliminated and liquidated. School teachers, intellectuals, politicians, former police officers, and otherwise rich or prominent people were specifically targeted for execution or especially savage treatment. For example, in Bratunac, that's KDZ605, P03205, paragraphs 80 through 82. Prijedor, KDZ206, KDZ523, KDZ4257. Sanski Most, KDZ340, P3634, pages 108 through 109. Vlasenica, KDZ044, and P107, page 26. Zvornik, KDZ029, P3195, paragraphs 22 through 24. Other evidence of the systematic elimination of Muslims in the manner evoked at these assembly sessions include evidence I alluded to earlier regarding a "standard cleansing operation," which included the instruction to kill any male Muslims encountered in the course of a cleansing operation. Similarly, in a June 25th, 1992 intercepted conversation which the Court has received in evidence - that's P1515 - we see a local leader instructing a military figure who's calling from another part of the municipality to: "... have them all killed there, please. All that is Muslim to be killed, like Alija. I don't want to see one military-aged Muslim alive there." A few weeks before that conversation, the same person had told another military figure: "I have a few years of schooling. We shall disappear. This is the struggle for survival." And he continued: "You know what a struggle for survival means. It's us or them." And his interlocutor said: "Exactly." And he continued: "Then we have to move dynamically in certain territories." To which the response was: "That's clear. That's clear." D1210. And, again, we see the linkage between the perception and fixation on being genocidal victims with the response in kind. Now, as I have noted, the accused did not solely promote the destruction of Muslims and Croats through speeches but matched his words with actions. He -- as I noted, he selected Mladic, who shared his view, and tasked him with leading that effort. He also relied on notoriously violent figures, such as Arkan, whom Ambassador Okun described as a leader of a particularly vicious paramilitary group and who the Court has heard about during the course of the case, including the approval of the invitation for him to appear from the Bosnian Serb leadership, including the approbation by Dr. Karadzic, and you saw that at P02848, pages 24 through 25. These -- such figures as Arkan and other paramilitaries were supported by and incorporated into the Bosnian Serb forces, at least until such time as their role in the subjugation and cleansing of Muslims had been largely completed and their criminal propensities began to turn back against the Serbian population. But their -- the recognition of them as genocidal was made explicit in a 28 July 1992 report by Colonel Tolimir: "Many formations of this type display hatred of non-Serbian peoples, and one can conclude without reservations that they are a genocidal element among the Serbian people." That's P2855. A further reflection of the intent of the accused in unleashing these forces for particular purposes. And, indeed, as this campaign unfolded, the accused ensured that the mechanisms of the Republika Srpska state structure that were nominally intended for law enforcement were not deployed to derail this genocidal effort. In the face of the mass violent crimes against non-Serbs, you've heard evidence that the accused not only chose not to have them prosecuted but to suppress any efforts to the contrary. And I turn your attention to P3773 and the conclusion that -- and the evidence that -- of the interference with the structures that would otherwise have been addressing such matters in pursuit or furtherance of the policy of an ethnically cleansed state. And the accused praised and rewarded those who perpetrated and promoted the commission of the underlying genocidal acts. And if you turn to P5525, the January 1994 ceremonial session of the RS Assembly, you'll see that after reiterating - again - the alleged genocidal threat posed by the "toxic all-destructive Islamic octopus," he praised the SDS, the Bosnian Serb MUP, parts of the JNA, the TO, and the VRS for "standing against our united enemies in a manner admired even today" and bestowed awards on a number of individuals whose names have appeared in the course of our evidence repeatedly, rewarded them for their role in implementing and overseeing acts addressing the Muslim and Croat population. And in those cases, implementing and overseeing the physical destruction of Muslims and Croats in Serb-held areas. Now, the Defence has argued, in part, that the evidence at its highest shows an intent to displace rather than destroy. And it is certainly theatrically possible to be faced with that stark contrast in various circumstances. But here, in this case, the evidence shows that thousands and thousands of non-Serbs were targeted for physical destruction, not for expulsion. Incident after incident in which a deliberate decision was made to physically destroy members of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat groups rather than expel them or allow them to flee in fear from Bosnian Serb territories. Now, we saw that in municipality after municipality, but I want to just address two of those municipalities. First of all, in Zvornik. And it's -- in so doing, I'm overlooking numerous massacres of hundreds of people at -- at -- not collectively but in -- in individual incidents. But I -- I -- I want to focus on two municipalities because I think they illustrate the point. So, in Zvornik, we see, among other things, the following. On April 9th, in the course of a takeover at Zvornik, 30 Muslims were found sheltered in a basement. The men were taken away and executed; the women and children herded onto buses and expelled to Serbia. That is KDZ023 92 bis, P65, P89, P92. At the beginning of June, several thousand Muslims from various villages were herded to the Bijeli Potok area. Approximately 750 men were separated from the women and children; the women and children placed on a buses and expelled. The men detained at Karakaj technical school where approximately 160 were killed and approximately 190 more were taken to Gero's slaughter-house and executed there. That's adjudicated fact 2744 to 756, KDZ029, and the testimony of Petko Panic. More generally, with respect to Gero's slaughter-house, it operated openly as an execution site and a collection point for hundreds of bodies of killed Muslims. And that's found at -- that's KDZ610, P4837, paragraphs 34 through 41, P3880, page 2902, and transcript 19142, and P3192. On 30th of May, soldiers rounded up approximately 150 Muslims from the Kosta Jevero [phoen] area, detained them at Drnjaca. Women and children were taken away, placed on buses and expelled to Bosnian Muslim territory. Men were taken to Dom culture in groups of ten and executed. Leaving the bodies of at least 88 piled up at the Drnjaca school playground. That's KDZ072, KDZ610, P4837, paragraphs 54 through 57. And the evidence shows that it approximately 2.000 Bosnian Muslim civilians were killed in Zvornik pursuant to an organised system that included not just mass executions but also the systematic transportation, collection and burial of bodies and cleaning of crime sites supervised by the Zvornik municipality authorities. That's KDZ610. That's on one side, on the eastern side. Let's turn to the north-west part of Bosnia and of RS territory, and that's in Prijedor, and let me recite some of what happened there. On July 23rd, killing of at least 16 civilians during an attack. That's adjudicated fact 1067, 1071, KDZ092, P702 through 703, KDZ014, and so on. And in July 1992, Bosnian Serb military and police forces conducted an attack on the Brdo area, which included villages such as Biscani and hamlets of Hegici, Markale, and so on. Bosnian Muslim population was ordered by the Bosnian Serb forces to gather at various collection pints. At one location, five unarmed men were executed by Bosnian Serb soldiers. 30 to 40 Bosnian Muslim residents of Markale were executed the same day. 12 persons executed in a field in Hegici by Bosnian Serb forces. 20 at a bus-stop between Alagici and Srmernica [phoen]. Following that assault on the Brdo area, Bosnian Muslim men were forced to collect bodies under the supervision of the VRS and between 300 and 350 bodies were loaded onto trucks. Almost all Bosnian Muslims and some Bosnian Croats. That's adjudicated fact 1071, 1077. KDZ094, P706, KDZ523, P4257, KDZ094. Following the attack on the Brdo, approximately 200 residents of the area were taken to Keraterm and detained in room 3. And a few days later, Bosnian Serb military personnel massacred at least 150 of these detainees with light and heavy weapons. And a fire engine was brought in to clean it up and remove traces of the massacre. That's adjudicated fact 1215 through 1219, KDZ367, P693, KDZ092. Around the same time, another large group from the Brdo area were taken to Omarska. At least 150 people were killed shortly after their arrival. Adjudicated fact 1185, 1191, KDZ048, P677 through 78, KDZ093. And around July 25th, a large number of Bosnian Muslim civilians detained at Ljubija, a minimum of 15 detainees executed there. Another 50 put on a bus taken to a nearby mine and executed by Bosnian Serb soldiers. Two managed to escape. Adjudicated facts 1186 through 1188, KDZ080, P3691, KDZ026 and 392, P2089 and P707. At Omarska, killings were routine. KDZ080 described counting dead bodies around the white house every morning. Numerous detainees were taken away and executed. For example, around late July, a group of 44 detainees were taken out, put on a bus, and killed. See -- adjudicated fact 1186, 1188, KDZ080, P3691, KDZ026, P2089, KDZ392, P707. An incident that Mr. Robinson referred to on Monday, around 21 August, approximately 200 men were taken away from Trnopolje and the surrounding area on buses in a larger convoy, and at Koricanske Stijene, the men were taken to the edge of a cliff and executed in groups. Dumped in the ravine. Later, there was an attempt to remove the bodies and cover up that crime. That's adjudicated fact 1243 through 1256, 2490, through 2492, KDZ523, KDZ038, Krajic and Komljenovic. And if you turn to P1483, a meeting of 27 May 1993 reflected in the Mladic diary, you'll see a reference to a discussion between one of the attendees at that meeting and the chief of the -- the former chief of police from Prijedor about concerns about what to do with the bodies of Muslims who had been buried in Tomasica mine. 5.000 Muslims. And the concern was they wanted to get rid of those bodies by burning, grinding or in some other way, and now General Subotic was involved, and they wanted to know what Mladic thought might be best by way of handling it. Your Honours, it is the dolus specialus that -- accompanied by the actus reus, the many, many acts, some of which I have enumerated, as we've discussed, that convergence that governs. There is ample evidence in this case upon which a reasonable Trial Chamber could conclude that the dolus specialus for destruction of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat groups, in whole or in part, existed. Finally, Your Honour, I'd like to turn to Count 11. During the course of their submissions, the Defence focussed a great deal on the issue of whether or not the UN personnel who were taken hostage were combatants or not. This is legally irrelevant. The Appeals Chamber has ruled that the prohibition against taking hostages in Common Article 3 embraces any person taking no active part in the hostilities, including members of armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat. That's a decision of 9 July 2009 at paragraphs 22 and 26 through 27. Even assuming that the accused reasonably believed that the detained UN members had combatant status, this could, at most, justify their detention as POWs with all the protections that would entail and could never justify their treatment as hostages which, in this case, included detaining them at strategic locations in order to render the locations immune from air-strikes, threatening NATO and UN commanders that further air-strikes would result in their injury, death, or continued detention and their physical mistreatment. Now, the Defence appear to argue that the crime of hostage-taking can only apply to a combatant if he is already detained with the intent to -- it is already detained when the intent to use him as a hostage arises. So, therefore, the argument seems to go, if the detained UN personnel in this case had combatant status, because the evidence in this case shows that their detention was directly linked to the threats to their lives and safety and was for the purpose of stopping the air-strikes, that this can't constitute the crime of hostage-taking. In other words, the Defence is essentially arguing that because these personnel were detained for the very purpose of holding them hostage, they cannot be considered to be victims of hostage-taking. Not only is this interpretation [indiscernible] absurd, but it finds no support in the relevant provisions of international humanitarian law. This interpretation hinges on the claim that a combatant taken hostage in this manner is not a protected hors de combat -- a protected combatant hors de combat. But the basic provisions of IHL define hors de combat in broad terms, and the key point is that the combatant has fallen into enemy hands and is in longer in a position to defend himself. So cite, for example, 1907 Hague Regulations, Article 23(C), which is implicit in the third convention as noted by the ICTR commentary to Protocol I, Article 41, and Additional Protocol I, as I said, Article 41. These provisions clearly classify as hors de combat a combatant taken hostage by the enemy. I think the Defence implicitly recognises that, because they turn instead to an argument based principally on the ICC elements of the crime of hostage-taking, and you recall that at transcript pages 28619 through 28620 and 28624, and the accused's claim is that prior detention must be a required element because otherwise the fourth and fifth elements of the ICC elements - that is, that the person is a protected person - and that the perpetrator is aware of the factual circumstances establishing that status would be redundant. Well, that is misleading. Because, even assuming that the ICC elements have some relevance here, the -- the -- the elements of hostage-taking under the ICC Statute that Mr. Robinson relies upon are the elements under Article 8(2)(a)(viii) and this Article criminalizes hostage-taking as a grave breach of the 1994 Geneva Conventions. The accused in this case, however, is not charged with hostage-taking as a grave breach under Article 2 of the Statute but, rather, with hostage-taking as a war crime under Article 3. So if the ICC elements are considered to have any relevance at all, then the elements of Article 8(2)(c)(iii) are the appropriate basis of comparison. And the status requirement under that article is that the person or persons seized, detained or otherwise taken hostage: "... were either hors de combat or were civilians, medical personnel, or religious personnel taking no part -- no active part in the hostilities." This requirement, Your Honours, is similar to the status requirement set out by the Appeals Chamber in this case. And drawing on the text of Common Article 3, the Appeals Chamber held that the prohibition of hostage-taking extends to any person taking no active part in hostilities, including members of the armed forces who have laid their arms and those placed hors de combat. And, again, we find that on the pre-trial decision, 28 April 2009, paragraph 65. So, if anything, the fact that ICC law also included those placed hors de combat as among the potential victims of a hostage-taking simply confirms our Appeals Chamber's holding that the status of detained UN members is irrelevant. Now, there's also a suggestion that prior ICTY jurisprudence supports that interpretation of the crime of hostage-taking, that the person must be -- the detained person must be hors de combat before the intention to use him or her as a hostage is formed, but while it is true that that the Blaskic and Kordic case dealt with individuals who were already in detention for some time, nothing in the Chamber's decisions and findings in those cases suggest in any way that prior detention was a requirement -- required element of the crime, and the decision, the pre-trial decision in this case and the Appeals Chamber decision, indicate quite the contrary. Finally, Mr. Robinson points to statements in the record by the accused referring to the detained UN personnel as prisoners of war in order to argue that the elements of the crime haven't been met and makes that citation at 28625. But it's -- it's difficult to reconcile his reliance on the accused's reference to the detained UN personnel as prisoners of war - that is, combatants who were hors de combat - with his argument that these detainees were not combatants hors de combat. But, in any event, whatever the accused believed at the time about the status of the detained UN members - and, again, I emphasise that has no legal relevance here - the evidence is clear that the accused and Mladic and other senior political and military Bosnian Serb leaders did not intend merely to detain them as POWs but, in fact, intended to use their detention in order to "gain an advantage or obtain a concession." And, again, that's the -- that harkens back to the elements in question as confirmed by prior decisions in this institution, including the decision of 28 April 2009. Intended to use their detention in order to gain an advantage or obtain a concession, just a few examples. In a June 21, 1992 videotaped BBC interview - that's P5026 - the accused was asked whether it was: "... a terrible mistake to have allowed your people to have captured UN soldiers, for the world to have seen them chained them, to have seen masked men holding guns at their heads. That was a terrible thing, wasn't it? Wasn't that an awful mistake?" And the accused responded: "Right. One mistake causes another mistake. One drastic move causes another drastic reaction. You have to realise that that was a reaction, not action, and we felt hopeless and helpless, and we had to do something very drastic in order to prevent further attacks and in order to show to the international community that we are cornered and that we, being cornered, are ready to defend ourselves by all means." Difficult to imagine a clearer acknowledgement, the elements of hostage-taking. Another example occurred at the 51st Assembly Session held on 15 through 16 June 1995 when the accused, referring to the hostages, stated that they were holding onto 15 of them until the end of the week in order to gain the advantage of keeping weapons in Sarajevo. And here's the quote: "We couldn't let them go all at once but in proportions. We even left 15 until the end of this week so we could keep the weapons we have in Sarajevo, knowing about the offensive and planning to do something in Sarajevo. Now any return of weapons is out of the question because of this offensive, so that, in a way, we even somewhat benefitted from this whole crisis." That's P1410, page 332. Just before this particular assembly session, the accused had ordered precisely that. In a 13 June 1995 order to the Main Staff, Main Staff commander and assistant commander for intelligence and security, the accused ordered the release of all captured UN soldiers at 1100 hours on 13 June 1995 except for: "... 15 military observers who shall remain in custody and prepare them for release scheduled to take place on June -- on Sunday, 18 June 1995, in the same manner as before." That's at P2156. And in a slightly more colloquial explanation of the purpose behind the seizure and continued detention of these UN personnel, you can turn to P2271, a conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and Momcilo Vinkovic on the 3rd of June, 1995. And here's what Mr. Krajisnik had to say about that -- so first, Vinkovic said to Krajisnik: "But, look, hold onto the hostages. That's a fantastic card. Don't ever forget that Saddam got destroyed when he released the hostages." And Krajisnik responded: "Yes, yes, we're doing that. We have an excellent method. We always have an ace up our sleeve." Mr. President, Your Honours, the evidence, including the evidence directly from those -- a number of those persons who were taken hostage, reveal quite clearly the -- that the nature -- the nature of their detention, that the elements of hostage-taking were met, and frankly the absurdity of an argument that one can't be guilty of -- responsible for hostage-taking because he has the intent to take them hostage. Mr. President, Your Honour, I'm grateful for the time to respond to the submissions made by the Defence. I still need to clarify one question you asked me before the session ended previously. With respect to P1412, that is, the 52nd Assembly I referred to, the quote that I referred to can be found at pages 23 through 24. Mr. President, Your Honours, that concludes the Prosecution's submissions. Thank you for attention.
